We follow the same procedure in flat space holography, where the spacelike curve sits on the cosmological horizon and the timelike curve lies between the cosmological horizon and timelike infinity. Evaluating the holographic TEE for a timelike interval in CCFT$_2$ on the plane, we find that, in contrast with the cylinder, the real and imaginary parts are equal.

papers.title: Modular Flow and Holographic Timelike Entanglement Entropy in AdS and Flat Holography
papers.abstract: Timelike entanglement entropy provides a useful probe of holographic theories, yet an explicit bulk realization of the modular flow underlying its timelike extremal curve construction has so far been lacking. We construct modular flows associated with spacelike and timelike intervals in AdS$_{3}$/CFT$_{2}$ and extend this framework to flat$_{3}$/CCFT$_{2}$. Beginning with the boundary symmetry generators, we explicitly derive the boundary modular flows and extend them into the bulk, providing a systematic procedure that relates bulk modular flows to the extremal curves and holographic (timelike) entanglement entropy. For spacelike intervals, the resulting bulk modular flows determine the extremal curves, whose integrated line elements reproduce the standard holographic entanglement entropy. We then generalize this approach to timelike intervals, explicitly constructing the modular flows whose fixed points reproduce the extremal spacelike and timelike curves, which give the holographic timelike entanglement entropy. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first explicit construction of the modular flow associated with a timelike extremal curve for a timelike interval. The same procedure is then carried over to flat$_{3}$/CCFT$_{2}$, which gives rise to the holographic (timelike) entanglement entropy. Finally, we show that the flat space results obtained in this work can be recovered from their AdS$_3$ counterparts in the flat space limit.

papers.title: Block Sensitivity and Certificate Complexity of Rotation Symmetric Boolean Functions
papers.abstract: We investigate block sensitivity and certificate complexity of monomial rotation-symmetric Boolean functions, obtaining exact formulas and structural classifications for several families. For odd-degree monomial rotation-symmetric functions, the equality $s(f)=n$ established in our earlier work yields $bs(f)=C(f)=n$. For quadratic monomial rotation-symmetric functions, we determine both measures completely and prove that block sensitivity equals certificate complexity. For consecutive quartic monomials, we determine sensitivity, block sensitivity, and certificate complexity in every residue class of the number of variables. Our principal result is an exact global block-sensitivity formula for consecutive monomials of every even degree $d\ge4$. Writing $n=q(d+2)+ρ$, where $0\leρ<d+2$ and $q\ge\max\{2,d/2-1\}$, we prove \[ bs(F_{d,n})=n-\min\left\{\left\lceil\fracρ{2}\right\rceil,d+2-ρ\right\}. \] We also establish the corresponding sensitivity formula by a self-contained argument, yielding arbitrarily large gaps between sensitivity and block sensitivity as the degree varies. For certificate complexity, we obtain exact pointwise formulas for structured run-and-gap configurations and establish additional global equalities, including $C(F_{6,8q+5})=bs(F_{6,8q+5})=8q+2$ for $q\ge2$. Our methods combine cyclic run decomposition, parity arguments, explicit sensitive-block constructions, and constant-subcube certificates. The exact global certificate complexity for arbitrary even degrees remains open.

papers.title: Sensitivity of Rotation Symmetric Boolean Functions via Binary Necklaces
papers.abstract: Rotation symmetric Boolean functions are important structured families in the theory of Boolean functions, where cyclic invariance permits compact algebraic descriptions while retaining nontrivial local behavior. We investigate their sensitivity through binary necklaces and monomial orbit sums. In the necklace quotient of the Boolean cube, ordinary adjacency does not record the number of coordinate flips: we give a directed flip-multiplicity formula involving stabilizers and distance-two near-periods, and derive exact local sensitivity formulas when the number of variables is an odd prime. For monomial rotation symmetric functions we determine sensitivity for all odd degrees and for quadratic orbit sums. For the consecutive-monomial family of every even degree $d\ge4$, we prove a run-cluster inequality and obtain the eventual exact formula $s(F_{d,n})=n-\min\{r,d+2-r\}$, where $n\equiv r\pmod{d+2}$, under the stated length hypothesis. The consecutive quartic case follows explicitly. We also evaluate sensitivity for cyclic run-threshold functions. Our results provide exact combinatorial and complexity-theoretic information about cyclic Boolean functions and clarify how cyclic symmetry governs local sensitivity.

papers.title: Equilibria and Consensus in Mixed Weighted-Average and Weighted-Median Opinion Dynamics: The Consensus-Promoting Role of Weighted-Average Individuals
papers.abstract: How individuals respond to their neighbors' opinions shapes whether a networked group reaches consensus. This paper analyzes synchronous discrete-time opinion dynamics on a fixed influence network, where individuals use either weighted-average (WA) or weighted-median (WM) opinion-aggregation mechanisms with individual-specific inertia coefficients. We characterize equilibria through graph-theoretic conditions on opinion level sets and WA balance equations, proving that every solution converges to a Lyapunov-stable equilibrium. We define type-dependent cohesive sets, whose WA members assign all their influence weight to the set and WM members assign at least half. The absence of two disjoint such sets gives a necessary and sufficient graph-theoretic criterion for consensus from any initial condition. Otherwise, an open set of initial conditions leads to persistent dissensus. Converting WM individuals to WA cannot create type-dependent cohesive sets and preserves existing guarantees of consensus from any initial condition. If the conversion eliminates every disjoint pair of these sets, the converted system also guarantees consensus from any initial condition. Four numerical studies examine the locations and proportion of weighted-average individuals, as well as the influence weights, while comparing the consensus criterion with finite-horizon simulation outcomes. In the four network ensembles with 100 individuals, the observed frequency of reaching a prescribed consensus tolerance is nondecreasing with WA proportion at each tested simulation horizon. This trend supports the consensus-promoting role of WA individuals, although individual realizations need not follow it.

papers.title: Cone Restriction Estimates under Half-Scale Dimensional Conditions
papers.abstract: We prove cone restriction estimates under half-scale dimensional conditions. Building on the framework of Du--Li--Wang--Zhang, we incorporate the broad restriction estimate of Ou--Wang and a localized multilinear estimate obtained through cyclic bilinear pairing and multilinear Kakeya bounds for local packet energies. For certain ambient and weight dimensions, our estimates are sharp in suitable ranges of $p$, up to an $R^\varepsilon$ loss.

papers.title: Low Lying Zeros of Dedekind Zeta Functions
papers.abstract: Let $K$ be a number field of degree $n_K$, and let $h(K)$ denote the smallest absolute value of the imaginary part of a non-trivial zero of its Dedekind zeta function $ζ_K$. In 1979, Hoffstein proved the unconditional bound $h(K)\leq 0.87+o(1)$ as $n_K\to\infty$. In a 1990 survey, Odlyzko announced the stronger bound $h(K)\leq 0.54+o(1)$ without proof. No improvement on Hoffstein's bound has since appeared with a published proof. We construct a comparison kernel from a linear combination of three identities and show that Hoffstein's original parameters give $h(K)<0.825$ for sufficiently large $n_K$. We generalise Hoffstein's method via Stechkin's trick and prove $h(K)<0.58$ for all sufficiently large $n_K$, giving the best proved estimate to date. Moreover, $ζ_K$ has at least $c n_K$ non-trivial zeros with imaginary part in $[0,0.58]$, counted with multiplicity, for some $c>0$ and $n_K$ large enough.

papers.title: Finite Root Sums in Symmetrizable Kac-Moody Algebras
papers.abstract: Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a symmetrizable Kac-Moody algebra with root system $Φ$. A subset $S\subseteqΦ$ is closed if $α,β\in S$ and $α+β\inΦ$ imply $α+β\in S$. For finite and affine Kac-Moody algebras, this closure property is known to extend from pairs to arbitrary finite sums that are roots. We prove that every closed subset of the root system of any symmetrizable Kac-Moody algebra is closed under arbitrary finite sums that are roots. The proof uses real-root strings, a simultaneous separation lemma for positive imaginary roots, and a lemma on when the sum of two positive imaginary roots is again a root. As an application, we extend a necessary condition for wideness of regular subalgebras from finite and affine types to all symmetrizable Kac-Moody algebras: the symmetric closure of the roots associated to a wide regular subalgebra is the entire root system.

papers.title: A Multi-View Low-Latency Direction-Sensing for Low-Altitude Network via a Multi-Armed Array
papers.abstract: Due to the directional antenna pattern, the received signal power decreases when the target deviates from the array boresight, degrading direction-sensing accuracy. Although rotatable arrays can alleviate this problem, repeated array rotations will induce an incremental long sensing latency. To break the dilemma of harvesting the directive gain from element and making a low-latency sensing, a multi-armed array comprising multiple subarrays with different orientations is proposed to provide wide spatial coverage encompassing low-altitude and terrestrial regions while enabling multi-view direction sensing. However, the different views lead to different direction-sensing accuracies. To fully exploit the complementary information from multiple views, two fusion methods, called SNR-weighted fusion and logistic-weighted fusion, are developed. The former directly assigns fusion weights according to the estimated received SNRs, whereas the latter employs an exponential SNR mapping to further emphasize high-SNR subarrays. Furthermore, the Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB) is derived to provide a theoretical benchmark for the proposed multi-view direction-sensing system. Simulation results show that logistic-weighted fusion achieves better accuracy in the very low-SNR regime, while both proposed methods approach the CRLB at medium and high SNRs and maintain stable sensing performance.

papers.title: On Waring-Goldbach problem for two squares and higher powers
papers.abstract: Let $ν_1(n)$ and $ν_2(n)$, respectively, denote the number of representations of the natural number $n$ as the following form \begin{equation*} n=p_1^2+p_2^2+p_3^4+p_4^4+p_5^4+p_6^5+p_7^8, \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} n=p_1^2+p_2^2+p_3^3+p_4^4+p_5^5+p_6^6+p_7^8, \end{equation*} where $p_1,\dots,p_7$ are primes in both above cases. In this paper, it is proved that $ν_1(n)\gg n^{43/40}(\log n)^{-7}$ holds for every sufficiently large integer $n$ subject to $n\equiv1\pmod2$ and $n\equiv\pm1\pmod3$. Moreover, we also establish that $ν_2(n)\gg n^{43/40}(\log n)^{-7}$ holds for every sufficiently large integer $n$ subject to $n\equiv1\pmod2$. These results improve and enhance the earlier work of Andrade [1] and Wang-Tian [17], respectively.

papers.title: Comparing randomized trials: a formal approach
papers.abstract: Disagreements between randomized trials that address the same causal question pose challenges for the interpretation and synthesis of evidence. We sketch a causal framework for comparing the results of randomized trials that explicitly accommodates the possibility of trial engagement effects. Using counterfactual outcomes defined under joint interventions on treatment assignment and trial-related actions, we compare trial-native treatment effects with the effects transported from one trial to the population of another in a common target population. We show that standard conditions for transporting treatment effects across trial populations are not sufficient to guarantee agreement between transported and trial-native effects. Agreement additionally requires conditions governing how trial-related actions affect outcome across studies - for example, absence of trial engagement effects, equivalence of such effects across trials, or lack of interaction between trial engagement and treatment assignment. Our framework clarifies potential sources of disagreement across trials and extends existing approaches to study comparison to settings in which trial engagement effects may be present.

papers.title: Scaling Laws for Multimodal Data Mixtures
papers.abstract: Frontier AI systems are increasingly natively multimodal, jointly pretrained on multiple modalities, such as text, vision, and audio. However, the scientific understanding of the multimodal data mixtures used to pretrain these systems --- how much of each modality to mix, and at what potential interference cost to the others --- is largely absent or gatekept. In this work, we derive data mixing scaling laws for three modalities: text, vision, and audio. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly adopt Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, as MoEs scale efficiently and partially limit cross-modal interference. We therefore use MoEs to conduct 268 experiments ranging from 457M to 8.3B parameters, on up to 150 billion tokens. Our work leads to multiple actionable insights into multimodal data mixing for training MLLMs. First, compute optima are modality-specific: audio modality is model-heavy, favoring scaling parameters over tokens, while text and vision require balanced scaling of model size and data. Second, repeating vision or audio data beyond 2x yields negligible benefits. Finally, cross-modal interactions are highly asymmetric: vision strongly interferes with audio, whereas audio's interference with learning text and vision is negligible. Overall, we provide a principled foundation for understanding the multimodal data mixtures needed to train frontier MLLMs.

papers.title: ACED-Bench: Evaluating How LLM Agents Acquire and Act on Causal Evidence
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as scientific assistants, yet we still lack reliable ways to evaluate whether they can investigate a system rather than merely answer a prompt. A useful evaluation must let agents choose experiments, interpret finite evidence, and make causal decisions, while preserving objective ground truth. We introduce ACED (Active Causal Evidence and Decision Benchmark), a neuro-symbolic benchmark that separates the readable scientific surface from the formal causal world: natural-language scenarios describe the system, while a hidden causal model defines the data, the effect of every intervention, and the oracle answers. In ACED-Repair, agents diagnose a failing production system: within 15 experiments they must decide which controls to test, read confounded and filtered data, and recommend a fix, which we re-simulate on a hidden true objective. In ACED-Query, agents answer causal questions and make constrained causal decisions in worlds backed by categorical probabilistic graphical models. Acceptance on ACED-Repair ranges from 43% to 0% across 12 LLMs, while strong agents approach ceiling on ACED-Query's qualification questions. Tracing every experiment shows where investigations stop: most open-weight models test a true lever on its own in fewer than half of the worlds, the strongest models test the right levers but often miss the working dose or combination, and agents that do run a working fix almost always recommend it. No model reliably repairs systems with two independent causes or systems that need a subgroup-specific policy. These results suggest that reliable AI co-scientists need explicit support for choosing experiments, keeping track of evidence, and composing interventions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Rose-STL-Lab/ACED-Bench.

papers.title: TestPrism: Rethinking Test Evaluation Beyond a Single Reference
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents have advanced test generation across diverse programming tasks. However, the common practice of evaluating tests against a single reference solution overlooks alternative valid implementations and can overstate test quality. We introduce TestPrism, comprising 300 test tasks from 17 sources and 3000 candidate implementations, evenly split between valid and invalid solutions. Its primary metric, Joint Success Function, requires the generated tests to fail on the initial program state, accept every valid candidate, and reject every invalid candidate. Across fourteen baseline coding agent configurations, Joint Success Function reaches only 28.00%, whereas single reference success reaches 59.67%. Our analysis reveals missed behaviors, unsupported assertions, and faulty test construction. To address these weaknesses, we introduce TestHelix, which combines heterogeneous synthesis of test and repair pairs with peer cross validation and recursive self improvement (RSI). Across two models, TestHelix improves Joint Success Function by 8.67 to 9.00 percentage points over the native harness comparators in the TestHelix evaluation

papers.title: Quantitative Verification of Infinite-State Networks
papers.abstract: Many network protocols and distributed systems combine recursion, unbounded local state, and quantitative behaviour such as cost, latency, or reliability. Existing decidability results for networks of pushdown systems are largely qualitative, and do not extend to quantitative analyses, which must jointly track traces and weights. We present a framework for the quantitative verification of acyclic networks of weighted pushdown systems. Finitely summarising a recursive network component requires collapsing the infinite family of runs obtained by pumping its nested loops, and doing so exactly, rather than by over-approximation, is a standing difficulty. We give a class of weight domains where this is possible: pumping semirings, those in which the weights accumulated by such a family collapse to a closed form; informally, the domain must be unable to count iterations. The class admits domains with infinite ascending chains, such as the arctic semiring and downward-closed languages. Over these, we give a terminating saturation algorithm computing quantitative reachability exactly, resting on two ideas: segment tree algebras, a compositional representation of runs, and thermal extensions, which symbolically separate accelerated weights so that further acceleration remains exact. We use this to compute upward and downward closures of context-free languages uniformly, and to lift the algorithm to acyclic networks over "thin" pumping semirings, yielding the first quantitative safety and reachability analyses for networks of pushdown systems.

papers.title: Information Divergence and Endogenous Evolution of Asymmetric Information
papers.abstract: Standard theories trace information asymmetry to privately held information, heterogeneous signals, or costly information acquisition. We identify a distinct mechanism: otherwise identical rational agents observing a common Markov state at asynchronous times can hold different predictive distributions because their information differs in age. When the transition kernel separates information ages, independent Bernoulli observation arrivals make such divergence recur infinitely often almost surely, even with identical arrival probabilities. When agents instead choose costly updating intensities, independent update realizations can regenerate heterogeneous information ages among ex ante identical agents. In a stationary Gaussian AR(1) environment, the consequences depend on common staleness as well as the age gap: holding the gap fixed, older information raises individual uncertainty while reducing expected squared forecast disagreement and the value of certifying relative freshness. This generates stale consensus: low disagreement despite high uncertainty. With multiple ordered ages, costly certification supports partial-unraveling equilibria in which fresher types certify and sufficiently stale types pool. Under geometric information ages, more frequent updating weakly lowers the smallest and largest equilibrium disclosure cutoffs wherever positive-certification equilibria exist. The framework has implications for credit, insurance, financial markets, and multi-agent AI.

papers.title: The optimal information complexity of VC learning
papers.abstract: Steinke and Zakynthinou(2020) introduces the Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) framework of analyzing the information complexity of learning algorithms based on algorithm-dependent information-theoretic quantities. We study one of these quantities, the evaluated Conditional Mutual Information (eCMI). It has been an interesting question whether the optimal PAC guarantee for VC classes can be recovered from the algorithm-dependent analyses via CMI. And we show that it is possible to recover this guarantee by constructing a learning algorithm whose eCMI is of order O(d) in the realizable case, where d is the VC-dimension of the concept class. Specially, our algorithm is a randomized Majority-of-5 base learners with optimal in-expectation generalization guarantee.

papers.title: Taxonomic Classification with Tag Arrays
papers.abstract: We present a tool, KATKA, for taxonomic classification with tag arrays. Compared to Ahmed et al.'s state-of-the-art tool Cliffy ({\it Genome Research}, 2025) on the SILVA dataset from their paper and a readset similar to one of theirs, KATKA is faster, more accurate, much smaller and drastically easier to build.

papers.title: Nonlinear lower-tail large deviations at criticality
papers.abstract: We introduce general methods to derive lower tail large deviation principles, for a variety of nonlinear problems of combinatorial interest. These methods are especially effective in "critical" regimes, where the nonlinearities are not sparse enough for Poissonian lower tails (e.g., Janson's inequality does not provide a sharp tail bound), but the situation is not so dense that combinatorial effects dominate (e.g., we cannot directly apply the theory of hypergraph containers or the relative entropy framework of Kozma-Samotij). In particular, these are regimes where one expects interesting phase transitions to occur. Our results have a number of consequences related to subgraphs in random graphs, answering various questions of Warnke and Jenssen-Perkins-Potukuchi-Simkin. For example, consider a random graph $G\sim \mathbb G(n,p)$, and let $L_\triangle(n,p)=\log\Pr[G\text{ is triangle-free}]$. The first-order asymptotics of $L_\triangle(n,p)$ have long been known in all parameter ranges except the critical regime where $p$ has order of magnitude $1/\sqrt n$. We are able to fill this gap: for any fixed $c>0$, we show that $n^{-3/2}L_\triangle(n,c/\sqrt n)$ converges to a limit expressed in terms of a two-parameter variational problem, which has a single phase transition at $c\approx 4.341$. In contrast, we show that there is no such phase transition for the probability that $G$ is $C_{2\ell}$-free, for any fixed even cycle $C_{2\ell}$. We also obtain some applications in combinatorial design theory. Addressing conjectures of Glock-Kühn-Lo-Osthus, Kelly, and Kwan-Sah-Sawhney-Simkin, we obtain new estimates on the number of order-$n$ Steiner triple systems with no Pasch configuration and the number of order-$n$ Latin squares with no $2\times 2$ Latin subsquare (both tight up to a factor of $\exp(o(n^2))$).

papers.title: When Should an In-Context Learner Expand Its Hypothesis Space?
papers.abstract: Learning systems adapt quickly within a familiar family of models. The harder step is deciding, from a prediction failure, whether opening a richer family is worth its cost. We cast this as a costly sequential decision and introduce the Structural Revision Environment (SRE), which produces matched failures from noise, exceptions, change within the family or structure outside it, varies the price of expansion and the remaining horizon independently of the evidence, and admits an exact normative solution of the one-shot decision. The solution shows that revision is a value boundary, not an evidence threshold: except at the lowest prices, the richer family becomes the more probable explanation long before expanding becomes optimal. Small Transformers trained in SRE reproduce the expansion boundary from utility alone. Pretrained 7B and 8B language models fail at a definite point: their predictions carry a failure-sensitive signal that their decisions do not reflect. Told the gain of expanding, they weigh it against price and horizon only when they reason, and the one model that finishes its reasoning on the history alone still does not estimate that gain. Controlled post-training of the small Transformers moves the prior and the sharpness of predictions, and neither moves the criterion.

papers.title: GPU-accelerated Regularized Vector Multiplicative Error Models for Positive-valued Financial Time Series
papers.abstract: The logarithmic vector multiplicative error model (log-vMEM) provides a methodology for modeling and forecasting multivariate positive-valued time series. However, the number of autoregressive parameters increases rapidly with the system dimension and lag order, posing challenges for estimation and model selection. This paper develops a regularized estimation framework for the log-vMEM with multivariate Gamma errors by incorporating hierarchical lag structures to induce sparsity and accommodate heterogeneous lag dynamics. We consider three hierarchical lag structures: componentwise, own-other, and elementwise, in combination with group lasso, adaptive group lasso, group MCP, and group SCAD penalties. Parameter estimation is carried out through an alternating block-coordinate optimization algorithm with sequential Gauss-Seidel updates, while GPU-accelerated numerical quadrature is employed to address the computational burden of evaluating the multivariate Gamma likelihood. Simulation experiments investigate parameter recovery and lag selection under different sparsity structures. The real data analysis is carried out on the realized volatility measures for Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) which allows a comparison of the competing regularization approaches in an empirical financial setting. Together, these developments provide a computational framework for sparse multivariate volatility modeling with flexible lag structures and dependent Gamma errors.

papers.title: Partially Dynamic Single-Source Shortest Paths in Almost-Linear Time
papers.abstract: We study $(1+ε)$-approximate single-source distances in directed graphs with positive integer edge weights in $[1,W]$. For every $0<ε\le1$, we give deterministic data structures for either edge insertions or edge deletions with total update time $m^{1+o(1)}ε^{-1}\log W$, where $m\ge n$ bounds the total number of initially present and inserted edges. Both structures explicitly maintain approximate distance estimates, answer distance queries in constant time, and identify unreachable vertices exactly. The incremental structure additionally reports a simple $(1+ε)$-approximate source path $P$ in $O(|P|)$ time. Our decremental structure gives the first almost-linear-time algorithm. It improves the previous best randomized expected bound of $\widetilde O(\min\{n^2,mn^{2/3}\})$ against an oblivious adversary [BPW20]. Our incremental bound improves the $ε^{-B}$ dependence of the $B$-level recursive algorithm of [Liu26] to an explicit $ε^{-1}$ factor while retaining almost-linear dependence on $m$. Our algorithms use modified interior point methods. For edge deletions, we extend the single-pair distance framework of [vBCKLMPSS24] to all targets simultaneously. A shared potential and one dynamic minimum-ratio cut instance support global updates to the distance labels. Our main insight is that constant relative cut balance certifies approximate distances at every target. For edge insertions, we develop an analogous circulation-based formulation implemented through the dynamic minimum-ratio cycle structure of [CKLMP24]. We also give a black-box reduction from distance estimates to path reporting in incremental graphs, with $m^{1+o(1)}ε^{-1}\log W$ additional maintenance time. This reduction may be of independent interest.

papers.title: Controllable Road Marking Generation
papers.abstract: Lane and road markings provide critical guidance for vehicle navigation and multi-agent coordination, yet authoring them at scale remains a manual workflow that limits quantitative analysis and scenario testing. We introduce Controllable Road Marking Generation, which synthesizes a missing center-region marking layout from a drivable-area mask, optional outer-ring markings, and a textual description. Our benchmark uses deterministic, metadata-derived prompts and three output channels: lane dividers, road dividers, and pedestrian crossings. We develop a conditional bird's-eye-view (BEV) pipeline that combines (i) a text-conditioned latent rectified-flow DiT trained with a topology-aware auxiliary loss, (ii) Gaussian-blurred training targets that provide smoother supervision for thin, sparse markings, and (iii) Structured Gaussian Render (SGR), a training-free post-process that recovers crisp divider geometry by extracting polylines, fitting cubic Bézier curves, and re-rendering them as anisotropic super-Gaussian primitives. On 4,597 Argoverse~2 test tiles, our system achieves Buffered F1 of 76.8 and clDice of 50.2, compared with 38.8 and 24.6 for an adapted mask-refinement baseline. When trained independently on the Waymo Open Dataset, it yields 88.0 Buffered F1 and 66.2 clDice. Component ablations show complementary connectivity gains from topology-aware supervision and SGR. Text-editing experiments reveal that stronger guidance improves edit success but also increases changes to non-target structures. We see this framework as a step toward simulation-ready road-marking variation, automated map completion, and early-stage infrastructure design exploration.

papers.title: What Does a Harness Repair? Four Preregistered Studies Around a Longevity-Tuned Language Model
papers.abstract: A harness search around a frozen longevity-tuned 1.7B model reported a rescue. An audit traced its gain to rows the start left unparsed and found that the caller sent reference answers as assistant turns; replication through the same pipeline missed this defect. We preregistered four studies and report every endpoint. In the first two, thinking off raised test accuracy over capped thinking in 7 of 12 cells, mainly by parsing rows the cap left unparsed, and was not meaningfully worse than a rescue in 7 of 9 small-model test cells. Replication reproduced an injected defect's distortion in 9 of 20 evaluable cases. At 14B, two GEPA harnesses beat thinking off by 34 test points but were not detectably above the strongest constant label. In the third study, GEPA beat the constant on FPB (confirmatory), thinking off was not meaningfully worse than any BoolQ harness, and 3 of 4 MMLU-Pro searches kept their seed; the fourth comparison was inconclusive on test. On exploratory Autocast, harnesses were within 0.7 points of the constant and gave one label in 93.1% to 96.8% of parsed answers on test. On the prediction tasks (14B mortality, Autocast) the harnesses ended near the constant label. The fourth study varied search-set skew and objective on CREAK and resolved Manifold questions. All its results are descriptive because render hashes were not committed before the first replication call (D001). Minority-recall estimates were lower at 80:20 than at 50:50 in all four test cells. The balanced objective and re-selection from each search's pool had higher minority- and lower majority-recall estimates in all four cells. Five of their eight minority-recall intervals included zero, as did all eight balanced-accuracy contrast intervals. This does not show that skew explains the earlier collapse.

papers.title: Distributed Learning of $α$-Potential Functions in Strategic Multi-agent Systems
papers.abstract: We study the problem of computing the tightest \(α\)-potential approximation of a general-sum game over continuous action spaces, within a prescribed class of potential functions and when each player has access only to its own utility function. The difficulty is twofold: the approximation error involves a worst-case search over an infinite set of unilateral deviations, and the required utility information is distributed across players. For a linear-in-parameters potential class, we use an exact finite-tuple reformulation that separates the problem into a global outer search over deviation tuples and distributed convex inner problems. We develop a primal--dual inner oracle tailored to this structure and establish a uniform one-sided accuracy guarantee. This oracle can be combined with global outer search to obtain an end-to-end guarantee on the outer optimization error. We also develop a projected zeroth-order outer method as a computationally lighter alternative for higher-dimensional problems. Numerical experiments illustrate the accuracy--computation tradeoff between the two outer-search methods and show that the proposed optimization framework can improve upon analytical \(α\)-potential constructions.

papers.title: Diffuse Galactic Backgrounds with SPHEREx: A Pilot Study of Background Modeling and Its Impact on Extinction
papers.abstract: We present a spectral analysis of diffuse Galactic background emission using SPHEREx data in a pilot Galactic-plane field, where uncertainty in the estimation of the diffuse infrared background is a major source of systematic uncertainty in extinction studies at near- and mid-infrared wavelengths. We construct channel-resolved background maps across the 0.75--5~$μ$m range using a Large Median Filter approach and then carry the extinction analysis forward only for the cleaner long-wavelength subset at $λ\geq 3~μ$m. In the present field, comparison against an earlier masked-median background model gives a median channel-by-channel background difference of about 6\% and a maximum change of $|Δτ_{\rm norm}|\simeq 7.4$ near 3.205~$μ$m, underscoring the importance of wavelength-dependent background modeling. These results demonstrate that spectral mapping with SPHEREx provides a practical framework for controlling diffuse background systematics and enables improved constraints on dust opacity and extinction in the Galactic plane.

papers.title: Integrated Imputation-Classification for Supervised Learning with Missing Data
papers.abstract: We study supervised classification problems with missing feature values. Existing approaches often decouple imputation from classification, producing imputations that may be plausible but uninformative for prediction. Instead, we propose the Integrated Imputation and Classification Network (IICN), which jointly trains an imputer and an ${(n{+}1)}$-class discriminator adversarially with a single class-supervised objective, where the discriminator learns to distinguish among the $n$ true classes and an additional ``imputed'' class. We prove that it admits a global optimum where the imputer and discriminator together implement marginalization over missing coordinates and yield a Bayes-optimal classifier. We evaluate IICN on FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10, and tabular datasets with naturally occurring missingness. IICN outperforms classical impute-then-classify pipelines and recent generative baselines, showing strong robustness and accuracy in challenging settings.

papers.title: No Einstein Relation, No Problem: How Relativistic Weakly Coupled Heavy Quarks Equilibrate Beyond Leading Logarithm Anyway
papers.abstract: Relativistic heavy quarks equilibrate even when their microscopic drag and momentum diffusion violate the Einstein relation. We investigate how equilibration proceeds as a function of the coupling and compared to simplified Fokker-Planck models. To do this, we present a detailed calculation of the momentum-transfer kernel in weakly coupled non-Abelian plasmas through strict $\mathcal{O}(g^4)$, and study the resulting dynamics at leading order in the inverse heavy-quark mass. Beyond leading logarithm, its non-Gaussian structure plays a crucial role in equilibration. We examine closely the analytic structure of the evolution kernel, determine the large-order asymptotics of the momentum-transfer cumulants, and show how the kernel's bounded analytic domain fixes asymmetric exponential tails at the level of the momentum transfer probability. Strongly coupled $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM also features an approximately Gaussian core and exponential tails, but differs in the nature of the kernel's singularities and the velocity dependence of the transport coefficients and tail exponents. These differences have distinct dynamical consequences: for the parameters studied, the persistence of the relativistic population in steeply falling spectra is largely explained by drag alone at very weak coupling, whereas fluctuation-induced survivor bias produces a large relative enhancement at strong coupling. Nevertheless, the shared qualitative structure between weak and strong coupling points the way towards a practical phenomenological description of heavy quarks anchored in first-principles field theory.

papers.title: Certified Mechanistic Edits: Behavioral Guarantees for Skill Removal and Preservation
papers.abstract: Mechanistic edits (ablations, weight edits, activation steering) are the standard tools for unlearning a harmful capability from a neural network while preserving useful ones. Current approaches validate their effects only by testing, which can never cover an entire continuous region of inputs. Prior work at the interpretability-verification boundary certifies descriptions of a model: what a circuit computes, or whether it faithfully explains the whole. We instead certify the behavioral effect of an edit: that disabling a circuit removes one skill and provably preserves another, for every input in a region; a feature non-interference guarantee in the information-flow-security sense. We demonstrate such certified edits from toy ReLU networks up to a standard softmax + LayerNorm transformer, proving removal and preservation over continuous embedding-space regions and reaching roughly 9x the input-perturbation dimension an exact solver can handle by switching to sound bound propagation. Furthermore, we prove that no finite deterministic black-box test can certify removal, exhibiting an edit that passes exhaustive testing yet provably fails on a survivor pocket that can be made arbitrarily small. Guarantees hold on small, standard-architecture networks and, like any removal claim, presuppose that the target skill admits a decidable specification, a property which real-world harms may not have.

papers.title: From Static Lindblad Stabilizability to Robust Physical Control Sequences
papers.abstract: We derive checkable convergence, error, and execution-cost bounds for repeating a supplied finite control sequence from a static Lindblad stabilization certificate and complete implementation data, including concurrent background dynamics. The static decay bound and error bounds from static to planned evolution and from the plan to execution together bound the actual cycle's contraction factor in one fixed Lyapunov metric. For target-preserving planned and actual paths and a controller returning to its initial state each cycle, a uniform contraction bound below one gives cycle-end convergence from every initial state under cycle-varying uncertainty. Uniformly bounded within-cycle amplification in that metric extends this convergence throughout physical time when cycle durations are bounded above and away from zero. With leakage, uniform error bounds relative to certified target-preserving paths give explicit long-time distance bounds. Cycle and within-cycle bounds also screen a specified finite hardware library for sequences certified to meet and maintain a prescribed tolerance. In a four-level cascade with finite pulses, calibration and timing errors, always-on dephasing, and bounded pumping, the selected sequence brings every initial state within trace distance $0.1$ of the target in one complete cycle of explicitly bounded duration and maintains that tolerance under repetition.

papers.title: Arbitrary Stage Spectra for Raikov Remainders Along Quotient Towers
papers.abstract: Let $θ$ be an ordinal and let $(N_α)_{α\leqθ}$ be a continuous increasing tower of closed normal subgroups of a Hausdorff topological group $G$, with $N_0=\{e\}$. Write $ρG$ for the Raikov completion of $G$, and put $K_α=\overline{N_α}^{ρG}$ and $H_α=GK_α$. The successive and limit differences of the groups $H_α$ mark the first stages at which points of $ρG$ become old quotient points. For every nonzero ordinal $θ$ and every set $S\subseteq(0,θ]$, there is a Hausdorff pseudocompact Boolean group with a continuous tower of closed normal subgroups such that every member of the tower is pseudocompact and the nonempty strata occur exactly at the stages in $S$. The terminal quotient can simultaneously be chosen isomorphic to $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$, and for every $δ<θ$ the successive factor $N_{δ+1}/N_δ$ is compact exactly when $δ+1\notin S$. Thus a tower may have a single nonempty stratum at a limit stage even when every successive factor is compact. For a closed normal subgroup $N$ of $G$, let $\widehat q:ρG\toρ(G/N)$ extend the quotient homomorphism and put $K=\overline N^{ρG}$. Over $gN\in G/N$, the fiber in $ρG\setminus G$ is $g(K\setminus N)$, homeomorphic to $ρN\setminus N$, while for $y\in\widehat q(ρG)\setminus(G/N)$ the entire $\widehat q$-fiber lies in $ρG\setminus G$ and is homeomorphic to $ρN$. For precompact kernels this gives a canonical decomposition, and nested quotients give the two-stage identity underlying the transfinite filtration. Further results concern pseudocompact Raikov remainders and include countable Abelian examples.

papers.title: Sequential Capacity of Quantum Processes with Finite Memory
papers.abstract: How complex can the responses of a quantum process become as it runs longer with fixed internal memory? We measure this complexity by sequential response capacity, the depth of an adaptive tree of experiments whose acceptance probabilities separate possible processes by a prescribed gap. Each experiment uses a fresh complete run, and one fixed process must realize every response along a path. For any fixed common visible dimension of at least two and internal memory cap, we prove that capacity has order $K\log((K+1)/γ)$ for $K$ transitions per run and probability gap $0<γ\leq1$. Time-dependent single-qubit phase channels without internal memory already attain the fixed-gap $K\log K$ growth, realizing each path with zero-or-one response probabilities. Under the same tester permissions, classical stochastic processes that measure in a fixed basis at every transition have only linear capacity at fixed dimensions and gap. For phase sequences selected by a classical address stored inside the process, we then quantify how known independent Pauli noise changes this logarithmic enhancement. With ideal tester controls and weak residual phase noise after correction, we prove matching capacity bounds at a fixed small gap. At fixed address size and fixed positive residual noise, the logarithmic enhancement saturates once the phase-sequence length exceeds the inverse noise scale, and capacity then grows linearly with sequence length.

papers.title: Universal Byte-Level Encoding: UTF-8/UTF-16 Routing to Reduce Cross-Script Token-Budget Disparities
papers.abstract: Byte-level byte-pair encoding (BBPE) tokenizers are attractive for multilingual large language models because they cover all Unicode text. In UTF-8-based BBPE, however, many scripts start from a higher fallback cost than English: when no learned merges apply, a multibyte character requires multiple byte-derived symbols. We call this worst-case pre-merge cost the encoding floor. A higher floor can increase token counts and per-request cost while shrinking usable context. Changing the whole text encoding can reduce this gap but make already-efficient English spans more expensive in mixed-script text. Thus, we propose Universal Byte-Level Encoding (UBE), a dual-alphabet tokenizer that keeps 1-2-byte UTF-8 characters in UTF-8 and routes 3-4-byte characters through UTF-16. This lowers the encoding floor for 3-byte Basic Multilingual Plane characters, used by many scripts that need more tokens than English, without raising it for any character. UBE changes only the symbols presented to byte-pair encoding, and a Unicode 17 audit confirms exact round trips for every scalar value and every input in three official test suites. UBE also composes with other boundary policies and morphology-based encodings. Across intrinsic evaluations, UBE lowers dispersion in English-normalized token-count ratios (Gini 6-14% lower on FLORES-200 at 16K-64K), reducing cross-lingual token-budget disparity. In multilingual language models, UBE matches BBPE's quality. In the main multilingual settings, UBE reduces token counts most where they are highest and also lowers English counts, yielding more usable context and faster prompt processing in content-matched benchmarks. Byte-level models benefit directly: UBE shortens their inputs by 29-33% in all 39 of the FLORES-200 languages written mostly in 3-byte characters (1.4-1.5 times as much text per context window), lowers byte-level Gini by 28%, and lengthens no input.

papers.title: Why Does Train-Validation Separation Emerge? Update-Pressure Density Dynamics in Pretrained Backbones
papers.abstract: During fine-tuning, training accuracy often continues to improve after validation accuracy levels off, widening the empirical gap. We propose a support-transfer account: early updates reuse broadly shared structure, while later fitting relies increasingly on narrower structure with less benefit for held-out examples. From fixed training probes, we normalize per-example gradient magnitudes and measure their pooled dispersion, $D_{\mathrm{den}}$, and their probe-count-weighted within-class dispersion, $D_{\mathrm{within}}^{\mathrm{wt}}$. A local model gives conditions for dispersion and directional cross-entropy separation to grow together, separating uniform logit scaling; additional decision-boundary conditions characterize accuracy-gap growth. A controlled five-level hierarchy tests the effect of sample-private support. A 240-branch intervention matrix crosses training-progress anchors, batch sizes, private shares, and gradient-differentiation doses. The negative gap dose response is clearer at later training stages and is retained across the four batch sizes. A further 48 branches replicate its direction across additional seeds at a fixed stage and batch. Both normalized readouts are positively associated with the accuracy gap in all 90 language fine-tuning runs across three backbones and six tasks. The same direction holds in all 20 vision runs across four datasets. Together, the controlled hierarchy, targeted intervention, and real-model trajectories support a connection between evolving gradient differentiation and train-validation separation.

papers.title: Second-order Wasserstein response for Lévy laws
papers.abstract: Moving an atom and splitting it symmetrically can give the same weak change in a Lévy characteristic, yet produce Wasserstein errors of different orders. We explain this through first- and second-order expansions of the distribution function for infinitely divisible laws with a Gaussian factor. The expansions are uniform over Lipschitz tests and include distributional directions from moving atoms. When the first response is nonzero, analyticity gives the signed second coefficient of the Wasserstein--1 distance. When it vanishes, a finite second displacement moment gives a quadratic response, with a positive coefficient whenever the dispersion is nonzero. For local balanced remeshing, we prove matching bounds in terms of grid-alignment variance and construct a linear program with a controlled optimization gap. We also determine the sharp transition as Gaussian smoothing vanishes. The appendices give proofs, metric speed and length, and multivariate and state-dependent extensions.

papers.title: Conditional Fluctuations of Mean-Field Systems with Stable Common Noise
papers.abstract: We study conditional fluctuations of smooth mean-field systems on a torus with symmetric stable common jumps of index $0<α<1$. A positive-strip estimate makes empirical Poisson acceptance errors negligible at the sampling scale. Given the full Poisson master, the conditional laws converge in probability to a centered Gaussian kernel in a negative Sobolev path space. In dimension one, quantile coupling preserves this limit for microscopic marks with relative tail remainder $O(x^{-ρ})$, where $ρ>\tfracα{2}$. A second-order tail expansion identifies the response when this condition fails: it shifts the conditional Gaussian mean at criticality and, when nonzero, dominates sampling below criticality. We also identify the transition from a stable to a Brownian rank error. In a translation model, rank and clock couplings give the same microscopic laws but different path fluctuations. Rank coupling gives a functional Gaussian limit. Clock coupling admits no diverging additive path normalization at the limiting center.

papers.title: Seamless Reconfiguration for DAG-BFT (Technical Report)
papers.abstract: Byzantine Atomic Broadcast in Asynchronous networks has been studied extensively for decades. In a fully asynchronous system with even one possible crash failure, the FLP impossibility result rules out deterministic consensus, motivating randomized protocols that achieve termination with probability one. More recently, DAG-Rider popularized a new abstraction in which processes continuously reliably broadcast blocks to construct a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) and then locally derive a total order using a randomized perfect coin. This separation of dissemination from ordering has renewed interest in asynchronous DAG-based Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) and inspired numerous protocols that improve expected latency or throughput. Reconfiguration, however, remains largely unexplored. Existing DAG-based BFT protocols generally assume a static set of processes, whereas deployed systems must occasionally add or remove nodes in response to operational demands. Existing solutions are not seamless; they either pause the system or delay membership changes until a predetermined epoch boundary. This may be impractical and can introduce downtime. A single agreed switching round is difficult to use seamlessly: by the time processes learn it, the dissemination layer may already have advanced beyond it. In this work, we present a seamless reconfiguration protocol for Asynchronous DAG-based Byzantine Atomic Broadcast. Our protocol allows the DAG to continue growing while the membership and corresponding quorum thresholds change, without halting the system. To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first protocol to provide seamless reconfiguration for DAG-based Byzantine atomic broadcast in a fully asynchronous network.

papers.title: Complete Factorial Asymptotics and Integrable Structure of Generalized Charlier Recurrence Coefficients
papers.abstract: We investigate the recurrence coefficients of monic generalized Charlier polynomials for the weight $ρ_μ(k)=μ^k/(k!)^2$, $μ>0$. The coefficients satisfy a discrete Painlevé reduction, and their deviations from the limiting values $β_n\sim n$ and $γ_n\simμ$ occur on a factorial rather than algebraic scale. A comparison with the recessive solution $J_n(2\sqrtμ)$ of the associated discrete Bessel equation, together with a Hankel-determinant sector decomposition, identifies the connection constant as one. For fixed $μ>0$, this gives $β_n-n\simμ^{n+1}/[n!(n+1)!]$ and $μ-γ_n\simμ^{n+1}/(n!)^2$. We further derive a uniform expansion for the normalized sector factor $Φ_n(μ)=e^{-μ}\mathcal R_n(μ)$, valid for $0<μ\le cn$ with each fixed $c<1$: $\logΦ_n(μ)=μ[(n/(n+1))^2-1] -μ^2(2n-1)/[2(n+1)^4] +O_c(μ(1+μ)^{3/2}/n^4)$. The proof uses transition-content moments for Plancherel growth and weighted Poisson-tail estimates. It yields joint refinements of both recurrence coefficients in the subcritical linear regime. We distinguish these quantitative asymptotic results from the classical Painlevé, Toda, and Young-diagram identities on which the analysis rests.

papers.title: On the quadratic length of plane Cremona maps of degree 4
papers.abstract: Every non-linear plane Cremona map can be decomposed into quadratic maps, and the minimum number of quadratic maps required is called its quadratic length. It is known that plane Cremona maps of degree 3 have quadratic length either 2 or 3. In this paper, we study the quadratic length of plane Cremona maps $φ$ of degree 4. Recall that either $φ$ is de Jonquières, i.e. it has a base point of multiplicity 3, or it is not de Jonquières. In the latter case, $φ$ has quadratic length 2, whereas in the former case we prove that $φ$ has quadratic length 3, 4, or 5, and we classify those maps that reach the upper bound.

papers.title: From Search to Signal: Search-Value Credit for Evolutionary Automatic Heuristic Design
papers.abstract: Large language models generate candidate programs for automatic heuristic design, while evolutionary search evaluates and selects them to guide further generation. Online post-training uses rewards from candidate evaluations to adapt the generator. Retained programs can also guide later generation as parents. This motivates rewards that reflect their reuse opportunities beyond immediate fitness. We propose Search-value credit (SVC), which constructs response-level rewards from actual admission to the retained set and a short-term parent-exposure proxy. Admission determines reward eligibility; the proxy weights eligible responses by reuse opportunities under existing parent-selection rules. Rewards are computed after candidate evaluation, without evaluating descendants. SVC retains the search and learning procedures of the Co-Evolution of Algorithms and Language Model (CALM) framework. Across four combinatorial optimization tasks with the same base model and response budget, SVC achieves the best mean final search performance on three tasks among six conditions. Under identical prompts and parents on traveling salesman and capacitated vehicle routing tasks, SVC-trained generators yield a higher mean proportion of responses whose programs outperform the best prompting parent than those trained with CALM's native reward. These findings support reward construction using search retention and selection information.

papers.title: Breaking the Bounded Entanglement Barrier for Quantum Position Verification
papers.abstract: Position verification, introduced by Chandran et al. (SIAM J. Computing 2014), allows verifiers to test a prover's claimed position by an interactive protocol. Classical position verification is impossible. Even for Quantum Position Verification (QPV), there always exists an LOCC (Local Operations and Classical Communication) attack if the adversary can hold an exponentially large amount of preshared entanglement. Somewhat surprisingly, we show that we can circumvent this barrier in the idealized continuous-time model, where time is represented by a real-valued parameter and challenge messages can be sent at a time sampled uniformly from a real interval. In this model, we give a BB84-based protocol that remains secure against any finite coalition of LOCC adversaries with arbitrary finite (possibly exponential) quantum storage and entanglement. Our construction can also be instantiated in the discrete-time model. Although prior impossibility results apply, our information-theoretic QPV protocol achieves any desired polynomial gap between the honest parties' total resources (communication and storage) and the adversarial resource bound. To our knowledge, all prior constructions that do not rely on idealized oracles required resources of the honest parties to be at least as large as the proven adversarial entanglement bound. Interestingly, the resource gap depends on the precision in measuring time. As clock precision improves, the adversarial resource bound increases while honest resources remain largely unchanged. We call this the "I sleep, you work" paradigm. Finally, we show that our techniques extend to an information-theoretic, position-based message authentication protocol, which in turn extends to an information-theoretic, position-based quantum key exchange protocol with the same guarantees as our position-verification protocol in the continuous-time and discrete-time models.

papers.title: Piecewise Parabolic Kinetic Energies and Classical Time Crystals
papers.abstract: We present explicit, exact analytic solutions for classical time crystals embedded in a parabolic potential for the position. While Lagrangians with a quartic kinetic energy yield complex trajectories governed by inscrutable elliptic integrals, we demonstrate that unconventional piecewise parabolic kinetic energies -minimized at nonzero values of the speed- admit simple, transparent periodic solutions. In these systems, the speed acquires definite periodic discontinuities but remains always nonzero. The requirement that the action be the smallest available determines the branch that the solution will follow, ensuring in addition that it is stable there and rendering the Hamiltonian single-valued as a function of momentum. Furthermore, we introduce a powerful piecewise parabolic emulation framework to approximate highly non-linear kinetic energies, demonstrating its utility on both quartic time crystals and the relativistic harmonic oscillator. We show that finding exact solutions to these emulated models provides accurate, physically transparent simulacra of complicated problems, offering a robust alternative to standard numerical approximations for non-quadratic kinetic energies.

papers.title: Marking Contour Tones in Yorùbá: A Typographic and Computational Proposal
papers.abstract: Yorùbá is a tonal language in which contour tones pose persistent orthographic challenges. These are especially notable for personal names and lexical items whose conventional spellings avoid vowel lengthening that would otherwise provide a host syllable for the second tone. A particular concern is a class of names in which the conventional spelling does not just omit tonal information but inverts the meaning of said name, sometimes asserting the opposite of what the name intends. This paper describes the problem, illustrates the inadequacy of current solutions, and proposes the adoption of the caron and circumflex marks. These are symbols with precedent in Yorùbá phonological scholarship since Olmsted (1951), used as orthographic conventions on single vowels to encode rising and falling contour tones, making them accessible for the first time through standard keyboard input and computational text processing. The proposal is supported by an implementation in the WriteYoruba keyboard and the TTSYoruba speech synthesizer, whose architecture and listener evaluation are reported separately (Tubosun, Oluokun, et al. 2026).

papers.title: Bianisotropic Space-Time Metasurfaces
papers.abstract: We experimentally demonstrate bianisotropic space-time metasurfaces based on varactor-loaded omega-shaped meta-atoms. Full-wave simulations reveal coexisting electric and ring-associated magnetic responses at the operating frequency, while a traveling-wave modulation drives reactive loads embedded in both responsive regions of the meta-atom. The resulting space-time modulation generates a reconfigurable polychromatic spectrum with directional sideband radiation governed by Floquet phase matching. Under free-space illumination, the same metasurface preferentially couples the received field toward one guided port, producing modulation-controlled directional routing. The measurements characterize the collective bianisotropic response rather than independently retrieving its electric, magnetic, and magnetoelectric susceptibility components. These results establish bianisotropic space-time metasurfaces as a platform for jointly controlling frequency generation, directional radiation, and wave routing within a single dynamically modulated aperture.

papers.title: Measuring Collapse and Correction in Homogeneous-Panel LLM Debate
papers.abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) debate is often evaluated by whether final answers improve, but a changed answer is not necessarily a better one: the same discussion can correct an initially wrong majority or collapse an initially correct one. Standard final-accuracy evaluations conflate these opposing transitions. We introduce an auditable protocol for homogeneous debate on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) that records each run as a transition ledger over collapse, correction, onset, and signed intervention utility. On 6,925 MMLU-Pro debates, the protocol records 253 collapses together with the corrections that offset them, and the correction side changes how interventions should be judged. Replay experiments reveal the central tradeoff: freezing every debate prevents 251 collapses but loses 804 corrections under equal weights, and a leave-one-model-out probe-gated freeze that is tuned for net utility never fires, so collapse prevention alone can recommend the wrong policy. A compact pre-debate 8-probe screen is a triage signal: its unadjusted family-level association with conditional-collapse risk is high (G=7, Spearman $ρ$ = 0.893, exact two-sided p = 0.0123), but initial-majority accuracy is a close comparator ($ρ$ = -0.821; family partial $ρ$ = 0.767, p = 0.0877), so we do not treat it as calibrated or capability-adjusted prediction. Round-level traces localize many collapses to the first debate round, where early disagreement can precede both collapses and corrections. Reasoning-mode models, including one model at two reasoning-effort levels, also show both collapses and corrections. We release replayable schemas, coders, audits, cost cards, and zero-API rebuild scripts so future model rows can be compared under the same denominators and signed utility ledger.

papers.title: Delegation without Priors
papers.abstract: A principal makes decisions relying on the private information held by a biased agent. Lacking a prior over the circumstances that may arise, she seeks a delegation rule that minimizes worst-case regret relative to the complete-information benchmark. The optimal delegation mechanism governs two distinct margins: whether to depart from a common default action, and how much discretion to grant conditional on departure. This rule pairs the default action with an action gap, followed by a discretionary interval with randomized boundaries designed to balance regret across states. This structure is globally optimal within the class of all stochastic, incentive-compatible mechanisms.

papers.title: Rewarding Novel Deductions: Solver-guided Process Supervision for Logical Reasoning
papers.abstract: Logical reasoning remains a major challenge for large language models (LLMs), particularly on structured problems that require precise constraint tracking, consistency preservation, and multi-step deduction. This challenge is especially acute for small-scale LLMs, which are more prone to producing inconsistent, redundant, or brittle reasoning trajectories. Existing approaches for improving logical reasoning largely optimize for final-answer correctness, providing only weak supervision over the intermediate reasoning process. In this work, we propose SPRING: (Solver-guided Process Rewards for Novel LogIcal ReasoNing Step Generation). SPRING uses an SMT solver as a training-time verifier of intermediate reasoning steps to provide process-level supervision. It introduces the notion of a novel reasoning step, namely, a step that is logically valid, consistent with the evolving reasoning state, and not already implied by previously accepted non-contradictory deductions. Based on this solver-based assessment, it designs process rewards that encourage novel inferential progress while penalizing contradictory and uninformative reasoning steps. Evaluation across three logical reasoning benchmarks: ZebraLogic, AR-LSAT, and Knights and Knaves, and four LLMs shows that SPRING consistently outperforms base LLMs, outcome-only reward baselines, and Logic-LM. On ZebraLogic, SPRING improves puzzle accuracy by up to 49.71 and 15.43 points over the base LLM and strongest outcome-only baseline, respectively. On AR-LSAT, it improves overall accuracy by up to 64.43 and 11.39 percentage points over the base LLM and strongest outcome-only baseline, respectively. On Knights and Knaves, SPRING achieves up to 93.14 puzzle accuracy and 96.05 person accuracy.

papers.title: Hitting sets From Derivations: Waring Rank and Noncommutative ABPs
papers.abstract: We give an explicit hitting set of size $\operatorname{poly}(n,d,r)$ for the class of $n$-variate degree-$d$ polynomials whose partial derivative space is bounded by $r$, over any field $\mathbb{F}$ of characteristic zero (or large enough). In particular, this yields a polynomial sized hitting set for the class of depth-$3$ powering circuits. The proof extends to the setting of noncommutative ABPs and provides a polynomial sized hitting set (of matrices) for the class of noncommututive polynomials that can be computed by polynomial sized noncommutative ABPs (this was also one of the results reported by Open AI~\cite{OpenAI26} in their release on 6 Oct 2026). The main technical insight is the construction of a ``formal derivation'' and properties of the associated Wronskian with respect to this derivation, which was previously studied by Moura \cite{Moura_2004} in a very different context. The proofs in this paper are elementary and completely self-contained. AI disclosure: A subset of the stewards obtained a weaker statement (hitting sets for polynomials with bounded partial derivative space) during conversations \cite{astra_proof} with OpenAI GPT-6 Astra. Extensions of this idea to the broader class of noncommutative ABPs were obtained by the other stewards (via further conversations with Astra), prior to OpenAI's dump on 6 Oct 2026. The proofs presented in this writeup is a rewriting (in the authors' words) of the proofs for both settings obtained by the models in a form that we believe is understandable to researchers. Although the proof is technically identical to OpenAI's release, we believe this exposition is self-contained, simpler, and more valuable to the community. The absurdity of the situation is not lost on us.

papers.title: Schrödinger--Föllmer Actor--Critic: Diffusion Policy Improvement with Finite-Sample Analysis
papers.abstract: Diffusion policies represent multimodal action distributions, but a $Q$-weighted update does not specify how to sample from the resulting target distribution. We propose Schrödinger--Föllmer Actor--Critic (SFAC), an offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) method for Kullback--Leibler (KL)-regularized policy improvement through conditional diffusion. A minimax Bellman critic estimates the action-value function, which defines an exponentially tilted target policy. A Doob $h$-transform expresses this update as a correction to the reference diffusion drift. The target drift is a weighted conditional mean of Brownian-bridge labels. We fit it by weighted regression using endpoints from the current policy and pointwise action-value evaluations. In the small-update regime, the KL-regularized update follows the natural policy-gradient direction, and the Doob correction represents the same local change in the space of diffusion drifts. Under suitable conditions, we derive finite-sample bounds that separate the errors from critic estimation, weighted neural drift regression, and diffusion discretization through a reverse-KL actor bound. The average-performance bound depends explicitly on the comparison coefficients over the policy iterations. Across six D4RL offline-to-online tasks, the final scores of the $Q$-guided bridge-regression implementation exceed its offline initialization on every task and Cal-QL on five tasks. We also compare with offline RL and online-only baselines.

papers.title: On the hit problem of rank five
papers.abstract: Let $P_q$ be the graded polynomial algebra $\mathbb F_2[x_1,x_2,\ldots ,x_q]$ over the prime field of two elements, $\mathbb F_2$, with the degree of each $x_i$ being 1. We study the {\it hit Peterson problem} of finding a minimal set of generators for $P_q$ as a module over the mod-$2$ Steenrod algebra, $\mathcal{A}.$ In this note, we present the minimal sets of $\mathcal{A}$-generators for $P_5$ in the cases where the degree are sufficiently general.

papers.title: Multiple change-point detection via bottom-up scanning
papers.abstract: We study nonparametric multiple change-point detection for high-dimensional sequences, aiming to identify time points at which the underlying distribution changes. While many existing methods perform well when change-points are well-separated, their performance can deteriorate when structural breaks are densely clustered. To address this challenge, we propose gBottomup, a graph-based bottom-up framework for multiple change-point detection in high-dimensional settings. gBottomup constructs a hierarchical segmentation by proposing merges of adjacent segments and verifying them through an unmerge rule that combines absolute significance with relative local heterogeneity, thereby adaptively refining partitions and estimating the number of change-points. Simulation results demonstrate that gBottomup performs reliably across a range of structural configurations and is particularly effective in frequent change-point settings, where existing top-down procedures may lose sensitivity. We illustrate the proposed method through an analysis of high-dimensional sensor data from an experimental hydraulic system.

papers.title: A Log-Star Comparison Between Expectation Threshold and Fractional Expectation Threshold
papers.abstract: We proved a log-star comparison between the expectation threshold $q(\mathcal F)$ and the fractional expectation threshold $q_f(\mathcal F)$ for any nontrivial increasing family $\mathcal F$ on a finite ground set $V$ of size $|V|=N$. Specifically, we show that $$q_f(\mathcal F)\le64\log_2^*(N+2)\,q(\mathcal F),$$ where $\log_2^* x$ is the iterated logarithm of base-2. Using similiar methods, one can extend this result to the following stronger form: there exists a universal constant $C>0$ such that \[ q_f(\mathcal F)\le Cq(\mathcal F)\log_2^*(l(\mathcal F)),\quad q_f(\mathcal F)\le Cq(\mathcal F)\log_2^*(\operatorname{VC}(\min\mathcal F)), \] where $l(\mathcal F):=\max\{2,\max_{S\in\min\mathcal F}|S|\}$ and $\operatorname{VC}(\min\mathcal F)$ denotes the VC-dimension of $\min\mathcal F$. On October 7, 2026, OpenAI released a result proving the equivalence of fractional and integral thresholds, which supersedes the findings in this note. The authors are keeping this note for historical reference.

papers.title: PoEM: Predicting RL Outcomes from Existing Policies
papers.abstract: Foundation models are post-trained with reinforcement learning (RL) to maximize specific rewards, such as helpfulness, correctness, or instruction following. This post-training process is computationally intensive, sometimes unstable, and has to be run from scratch every time the reward model changes or when we want to combine multiple rewards. We hence ask: given a new reward function, is it possible to predict the policy RL would produce without actually training on that reward? We answer this in the affirmative by introducing PoEM, a framework for predicting RL outcomes using models previously trained on other rewards. First, we build on the fact that if the new reward function can be written as a linear combination of existing ones, then the optimal policy can be expressed as a combination of the existing policies in log-probability space. Surprisingly, even in cases where the rewards are not linearly connected, we observe that policies learned through RL often span an approximately low-rank subspace across rewards. To our benefit, the weights for this combination can be estimated using only the reward or basis policy outputs on the samples. We turn these observations into an algorithm that takes post-trained models and a target reward function, and approximates the target RL policy without any additional RL training. We experimentally evaluate our approach across programmatic and learned rewards for open-ended generation, with additional experiments on math reasoning, tool calling, and image generation.

papers.title: Anchored Extra-Proximal Methods: Optimal Higher-Order Methods for Monotone Inclusion Problems
papers.abstract: We characterize, up to logarithmic factors, the optimal higher-order oracle complexity of finding approximate solutions to composite monotone inclusion problems, formed by the sum of a smooth single-valued monotone operator and a maximal monotone set-valued operator. We introduce the Anchored Extra-Proximal (AEP) framework, which combines an anchored extrapolation step with an inexact anchored proximal update satisfying a relative-error condition. This framework recovers the composite Fast Extragradient method in the first-order setting and yields natural higher-order extensions through Taylor approximations of the smooth operator at the extrapolated point. For every $p\geq 2$, assuming that the $(p-1)$th derivative of the single-valued operator is $L_p$-Lipschitz continuous and the initial distance to a solution is at most $R$, we combine AEP with a bisection line search to obtain a $p$th-order method that attains a tangent residual of at most $\varepsilon$ in $\widetilde{O}((L_p R^{p}/\varepsilon)^{\frac{2}{3p-1}})$ oracle calls. We complement this result with a worst-case lower bound of $Ω((L_p R^p/\varepsilon)^{\frac{2}{3p-1}})$ for every deterministic algorithm in the $p$th-order oracle model, without imposing any prescribed update structure. For the subclass of smooth nonexpansive fixed-point problems, we further establish a lower bound of $Ω(\min\{R/\varepsilon, {(L_p R^{p}/\varepsilon)}^{\frac{2}{3p-1}}\})$. By choosing between AEP and Halpern iteration, we match this lower bound up to logarithmic factors, thereby also settling the deterministic oracle complexity of smooth nonexpansive fixed-point problems.

papers.title: On the $W^{2,p}$ solvability for mixed boundary value problems
papers.abstract: We establish global $W^{2,p}$ solvability for the Poisson equation with mixed Dirichlet--Neumann boundary conditions in two classes of domains in all dimensions $n\geq 2$. For $C^{1,α}$ domains with a Reifenbeg flat interface, we obtain the optimal range $1<p<4/3$, provided that $α>1-1/p$. For Lipschitz polyhedra with facewise boundary decompositions, we obtain solvability for $p$ close to $1$. In both settings, we establish endpoint $W^{2,1}$ solvability for data in an adapted atomic Hardy space. Applications of the methods to Lamé systems are also discussed.

papers.title: EvLink: Source-Grounded Evidence Linking for Graph RAG
papers.abstract: Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) supports multi-hop reasoning by organizing corpora into structured graphs. However, graph reachability often captures semantic association rather than evidence support, so a reachable passage may still fail to justify a required cross-passage transition. We propose EvLink, an evidence-linking retriever that preserves passages as retrievable evidence units and builds evidence-supported transitions between them. EvLink constructs two types of reliable links: relation-grounded evidence links justified by explicit source relations, and endpoint-alignment links serving as sourcebounded fallbacks. For retrieval, we introduce a two-stage retrieval strategy. First, bounded breadth-first search over source-grounded evidence links recovers bridge passages missed by similarity-based methods. Then, evidenceneed mining with noisy-OR coverage refinement selects a compact, non-redundant evidence set satisfying distinct question facets. Experiments on three multi-hop and two simple QA benchmarks show EvLink consistently outperforms leading GraphRAG baselines with average gains of 2.4 R@5, 1.9 EM, and 2.4 F1

papers.title: Finite-Sample Probabilistic Safety Certification for AI-Based Grid-Edge Coordination
papers.abstract: Coordinating a large population of flexible grid-edge devices can alleviate the need for time-consuming and capital-intensive network upgrades. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based control methods such as multi-agent reinforcement learning or imitation learning are promising to this coordination due to their real-time decision scalability. However, system operators still need an independent and rigorous way to decide whether a given AI system is safe enough for deployment. This paper develops a \emph{finite-sample} probabilistic safety certification framework for AI-based grid-edge coordination. The central idea is to reduce the complete input--AI--decision--evaluation workflow to a binary unsafe outcome under an operator-defined safety specification, and then use exact binomial inference to certify the corresponding unsafe operation probability. Given a set of held-out calibration scenarios, the framework returns the tightest one-sided upper certificate and an accept/reject deployment criterion that controls the probability of false safety certification. Because the certification is for the calibration distribution that may \emph{deviate} from the future operation, we further combine the nominal certificate with physically interpretable sample-space adversarial attacks, a concept widely used in AI models to investigate their fragility. Case studies on grid-edge flexibility coordination with 1{,}000-agent AI models (independent parameters) verify the safety guarantee and the value of integrating adversarial attacks into a rolling-window training-certification-deployment flow.

papers.title: When are bosonic Gaussian states classical to learn?
papers.abstract: A fundamental question in physics is: When does classical behavior emerge from quantum systems? Bosonic Gaussian states provide a natural setting to explore this quantum-classical boundary, as they capture both the classical field behavior and the intrinsic quantum nature of light. Here, we address this problem from a learning-theoretic perspective by asking: When are bosonic Gaussian states classical to learn? That is, under what conditions (if any) can an n-mode bosonic Gaussian state be learned with as few samples, and with operations as simple, as are needed to learn a classical 2n-variate Gaussian distribution?
