We argue that this target is arbitrary -- what truly matters is the ideal result, not the intermediate path taken to reach it. We propose IdealCache, a training-free framework that abandons step-wise imitation of the reference trajectory. Instead, it anchors caching on a per-input ensemble of ideal trajectories constructed from candidate target results, aggregates their geometry into a single graph, and discovers optimal non-uniform schedules via a constrained shortest path on this graph. By decoupling from the reference process, IdealCache breaks the performance bottleneck of trajectory-approximation; our schedules can attain near-lossless fidelity in generation and even surpass on task-specific metrics (e.g., maintaining higher semantic consistency in image editing). Without retraining, IdealCache achieves 6.35x speedup on Qwen-Image, 5.84x on Qwen-Image-Edit, and 4.32x on HunyuanVideo, with competitive or superior quality across tasks.

papers.title: Critical Branching Systems with General Lifetimes: Hunt Motions and Applications to Semilinear Equations
papers.abstract: We consider a critical monotype Bellman-Harris branching particle system on $E=R^d$ or $E=[0,\infty)^d$, started from a homogeneous Poisson field with Lebesgue intensity. Particles follow a conservative Hunt process with transition semigroup $(P_t)_{t\ge 0}$, have independent lifetimes with distribution $Γ$, and reproduce at death with generating function $f(s)=s+c(1-s)^{1+β}$. We assume Lebesgue invariance and uniform bounds $P_t1_K=O(t^{-q})$ for compact $K$. We also impose a localization condition: the expected number of particles in a fixed compact set at time $t$ descended from ancestors initially outside suitable regions of volume $O(t^q)$ can be made arbitrarily small, uniformly for $t\ge 1$. For spread-out lifetimes of finite mean, the system converges to a nontrivial limit of Lebesgue intensity when $qβ>1$ and becomes locally extinct when $qβ\le 1$. For nonarithmetic lifetimes satisfying $\barΓ(t)\sim c_1t^{-γ}$, $0<γ\le 1$, the threshold is $qβ=γ$: the limit is Poisson above it, local extinction holds below it, and a nontrivial subsequential limit exists at equality. We verify the hypotheses and determine recurrence-transience regimes for symmetric and anisotropic stable processes, symmetric uniformly elliptic diffusions, generalized squared-Bessel products on $[0,\infty)^d$, and symmetric bilateral Bessel-type diffusions on $R^d$ and their nonsingular linear images. Finally, we derive quantitative sufficient conditions for survival of total mass in semilinear equations with absorption, including time-dependent diffusion rates. Here survival means that the limiting total mass is strictly positive. For a hyperbolic diffusion, this holds for every $β>0$ in the absorption term $-v^{1+β}$.

papers.title: On the universal structure in deterministic generative diffusion
papers.abstract: Diffusion-based generative modeling has emerged as a general computational framework for simulating high-dimensional, structured data across various domains. Understanding its generative mechanisms is paramount for advancing model training and inference in a principled way. Here, we demonstrate that deterministic sampling trajectories share a universal geometric structure invariant to data modalities and diffusion model implementations. This structure can be largely explained by an exactly solvable model based on the optimal linear denoiser.

papers.title: TimeTraveler: Temporal Strategy Planning with Time Dictionary for Streaming Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding (SVU) requires models to answer user queries over continuously evolving video streams. Unlike offline video QA, SVU must handle queries whose evidence may lie in the past, appear in the current scene, or emerge only after future observations. Existing streaming video systems often rely on compact visual memories or fixed evidence-access schemes, which can lose fine-grained details and fail to adapt the answering process to the temporal intent of each query. In this paper, we propose TimeTraveler, a streaming VQA framework that performs temporal strategy planning with a Time Dictionary. Inspired by the need to search across different temporal regions of a stream, TimeTraveler stores each observed moment as a timestamp-indexed structured caption and uses this dictionary as an explicit source of queryable evidence. Given a query, TimeTraveler determines whether to recall past evidence, read the present context, or wait for future observations, and then applies a strategy-specific evidence acquisition process. Comparative experiments on streaming video QA benchmarks show that TimeTraveler improves streaming question answering by preserving fine-grained temporal evidence and selecting the appropriate temporal strategy for each query. The project page is available at https://geppa.github.io/TimeTraveler.

papers.title: Vázquez Strong Maximum Principle and Compact Support Principle for singular and degenerate elliptical operators
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present adaptations of the classical strong maximum principle and the compact support principle for a certain class of equations, with particular emphasis on the degeneracy of fully nonlinear operators and a new Vázquez-type condition on the nonhomogeneous term. The novelty of our approach lies in the framework of the problem: the coefficients of the operators are bounded, but we introduce a degeneracy depending on the power of the gradient of the solution. Moreover, the source term $f$ on the right-hand side of the equation is treated under a adapted and optimal integrability assumptions.

papers.title: Two-Sided Conformal Evidence Sets for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can surface passages that support a claim, contradict it, or fail to address it, yet existing calibrated grounding methods are typically one-sided and model only supporting evidence. We introduce Conformal Evidence Sets (CES), a two-sided framework that returns separate support and refutation sets with finite-sample inclusion coverage of at least $1-α$ on each side under exchangeability; a Bonferroni union yields joint coverage of at least $1-2α$. On labeled candidate pools from the contrastive VitaminC benchmark, CES closely tracks nominal coverage across $α\!\in\!\{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20,0.30\}$, with maximum deviations of $3.0$ percentage points for support and $5.4$ for refutation, and reaches essentially the same empirical coverage--size frontier as a test-tuned fixed-threshold heuristic without any test exposure. Stress tests mark the boundary of that guarantee: under FEVER distribution shift both sides under-cover, by up to $12.7$ percentage points, and support-side group-stratified recalibration substantially reduces the support gap. Scorer swaps, hard-negative retrieval, cross-dataset transfer, and a live end-to-end pilot expose a clear separation: when exchangeability holds and relevant evidence is retrieved, evidence inclusion remains calibrated even with an imperfect scorer, whereas the support/refute verdict tracks scorer quality directly. Calibrated evidence coverage and reliable verdicts are therefore distinct properties and should be reported separately.

papers.title: Reproducible LoRA Inference Through Deterministic Split-K Reduction
papers.abstract: Reproducibility is important for LoRA-adapted language models used in repeated evaluation, auditing, and decision-making. However, Split-K kernels used to introduce parallelism in low-rank LoRA multiplications can have the unintended consequence of numerical nondeterminism when partial results are combined using floating-point atomic additions. We investigate this non-determinism in vLLM across GSM8K mathematical reasoning, MBPP code generation, and Jev-style structured toxicity decisions on Civil Comments and introduce a deterministic Triton Split-K implementation. Under identical-input replay, Atomic Split-K=8 produces different FP32 shrink outputs in 97.61% of comparisons, while our Deterministic Split-K=8 shows no observed variation. Repeated atomic inference changes generated outputs in 17.30% of GSM8K and 14.96% of MBPP comparisons, sometimes altering task correctness. Structured-decision probabilities vary in 81.47% of atomic comparisons, with decision flips. Controlled tracing demonstrates how shrink-output differences propagate into the KV cache and how accumulated cache differences can change token decisions and final answers. Our deterministic Triton Split-K=8 implementation preserves parallelism, achieving 16.8-21.1% latency-based speedup over unsplit reduction with only 1.02-2.62% additional latency relative to Atomic Split-K=8.

papers.title: Objective Diversification of Dynamic Hedging
papers.abstract: A hedging objective reflects the risk preference of the hedger, so the conventional approach is to estimate the hedge ratio directly under the chosen objective. This paper asks whether that estimate should be used alone. We construct five objective-specific rolling hedge-ratio estimators---minimum variance, least absolute deviation (LAD), downside semivariance, lower-tail quantile, and Expected Shortfall (ES)---from the same historical stock--market returns, and combine the resulting estimates under a fixed final evaluation objective. Separate multi-output ExtraTrees models predict the within-stock-date ranks of the five candidates under MSE, LAD, downside semivariance, and 10\% quantile loss. The design uses pre-specified 60-, 90-, 120-, and 180-day windows with objective-matched rolling estimators as benchmarks. Adaptive weighting improves the corresponding loss in all sixteen objective--window comparisons. Equal weighting, which uses the same objective-specific hedge ratios without state variables or learned reweighting, already improves downside and quantile hedging. The results therefore suggest that estimates generated under other objectives can be useful even when the final hedging preference and evaluation objective are fixed, while adaptive weighting can provide a further improvement.

papers.title: On the Vázquez Strong Maximum Principle for Linear and Nonlinear Elliptic Equations with Unbounded Coefficients and Optimal Conditions
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present adaptations of the classical strong maximum principle for a certain class of equations, with particular emphasis on linear operators in non-divergence form and a new strategy to prove it. The novelty of our approach lies in the setting of the problem: the coefficients of the operators are unbounded, assumed to be merely integrable in the $L^{p,q}$-sense, and the source term $f$ on the right-hand side of the equation is treated under optimal integrability assumptions.

papers.title: Evaluating classification and explainability in multimodal petrographic image analysis
papers.abstract: Automated thin-section classifiers increasingly combine plane-polarised and cross-polarised light (PPL and XPL), two complementary views central to petrographic identification. Classification accuracy alone does not reveal whether model errors reflect mineralogical relationships, how predictions depend on each optical view, or whether attribution maps identify regions that influence model decisions. Here, we examine these complementary aspects of the released LITHOS dual-stream vision transformer using outputs from an earlier evaluation of 105,802 expert-annotated grains across 25 categories. Classification errors frequently followed the label taxonomy: 72.6\% of misclassified plagioclase, microcline and sanidine grains were assigned the generic Feldspar label, while 87.1\% of quartz-family grains received a label within that family, compared with 66.6\% assigned their exact label. Replacing the XPL input with its per-channel spatial means produced a greater reduction in true-class probability than equivalent PPL replacement in 20 of 25 categories, but not in the three quartz categories. Five explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) attribution procedures generated visually distinct maps for identical inputs. In a superpixel-deletion analysis involving 30 grains from 29 thin sections, method-minus-random contrasts ranged from $-0.043$ to $0.057$, with all 41 simultaneous 95\% confidence intervals including zero. Together, these findings show that error structure, modality sensitivity and attribution behaviour capture distinct aspects of model performance that cannot be established from classification accuracy or visual inspection of attribution maps alone.

papers.title: Simple proof of conditions requiring maximal entanglement for local state verification and discrimination
papers.abstract: For deterministic state verification by separable measurements, the Schmidt rank of an entangled resource must be at least that of the state being verified [N. Yu, R. Duan, and M. Ying, IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 60, 2069 (2014)], and if the two are equal, the resource must be maximally entangled [S. Akibue, J. Miyazaki, and H. Osaka, Lett. Math. Phys. 116, 110 (2026)]. The latter was derived from a general theorem proved using algebraic geometry. In this paper, we give a simple, self-contained proof of both statements using only linear algebra. We then use these results to show that among pure entangled resources of local dimension at most $d$, a maximally entangled state of $\mathbb{C}^d\otimes\mathbb{C}^d$ is necessary and sufficient for perfect local discrimination of a generic orthogonal basis of $\mathbb{C}^d\otimes\mathbb{C}^d$, however weakly entangled. The same holds for local implementation of a generic orthogonal measurement.

papers.title: Regret Equals Integrated Covariance: Exact Identities for the Value of Information in Stochastic Optimization
papers.abstract: For a stochastic program $\min_{z\in Z} c^T z + h(z)$ with a random cost vector $c$, regret, or the expected value of perfect information, is usually computed by re-solving the problem scenario by scenario. We show that regret is determined by the covariance between the cost vector and the optimal decision $π^s(c)$. The identity is exact and holds without regularity assumptions once the covariance is integrated along the path from the mean to each scenario. With $c_s=E[c]+s(c-E[c])$, $Reg=-\int_0^1 s^{-1} Cov(c_s,π^s(c_s))\,ds$. Three consequences follow. First, the plain covariance is always an upper bound: $0\le Reg\le-Cov(c,π^s(c))$. Second, when the optimal decision rule is affine, as in unconstrained and equality-constrained (e.g., budget-constrained Markowitz) quadratic programs, regret equals exactly one half of the covariance. For purely linear objectives, an affine rule forces zero regret. Third, the ratio of regret to covariance lies in $[0,1]$ and is governed by the shape of the covariance profile along the path. The noise level at which this profile first becomes positive is a decision-stability margin that tightens the bound. The identity also holds scenario by scenario for any predicted cost, so it applies to linear and combinatorial programs with discontinuous decision rules. We give dimension-free concentration bounds and a central limit theorem for the plug-in estimator. Across 7 problem classes, 8 cost distributions, and the shortest-path benchmark of Elmachtoub and Grigas (2022) with $10^6$ draws per configuration, the identities hold to within quadrature error, and the covariance bound holds in every scenario.

papers.title: A Multidimensional Evaluation Framework for Artificial Intelligence-Based Ocean State Forecasts
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) based ocean state forecasts now approach or surpass those produced by operational ocean forecasting systems as measured by conventional pointwise metrics. However, these metrics may favor spatially smoothed forecasts and cannot determine whether forecast variables remain physically coherent. Forecast evaluation should therefore move beyond overall pointwise accuracy toward assessing forecast trustworthiness. We propose a multidimensional framework comprising overall pointwise accuracy, physical consistency, and distributional consistency. Overall pointwise accuracy summarizes forecast and reference agreement over all valid samples; physical consistency evaluates dynamical balances using model outputs alone; and distributional consistency evaluates distribution tails and multiscale spatial structures. Three AI models were deployed as representative testbeds in a unified operational environment. This comprehensive assessment shows that lower overall pointwise errors cannot preclude substantial dynamical imbalances and suppressed fine-scale variance. Conversely, higher pointwise errors may arise from spatial displacement of coherent structures rather than a poor representation of their amplitude. The results demonstrate that the evaluation of AI ocean forecasting models should be based on the multi-dimensional assessment of forecast trustworthiness, rather than solely relying on a single metric. The study provides a preliminary framework for AI model intercomparison, which is also informative for targeted model refinement and operational implementation.

papers.title: UniFlow: Unified Multi-Scale Flow Matching for Time Series Generation
papers.abstract: Real-world time series exhibit complex dynamics across multiple temporal resolutions, yet effectively incorporating multi-scale information into generative modeling remains challenging without increasing generative complexity. We propose UniFlow, a unified framework that integrates multi-scale representation learning with efficient non-autoregressive generation through a shared-semantic discrete interface. Specifically, a multi-scale tokenizer employs shared-index voting to consolidate complementary temporal information into a single public-ID sequence, while scale-specific codebooks preserve the information required for reconstruction. Building on this unified representation, we develop geometry-aware categorical flow matching, which initializes transport from learned low-rank anchors and generates public identities non-autoregressively. This design captures multi-scale temporal structure without requiring multiple generative token streams or sequential token decoding. Experiments across four benchmarks and both short- and long-term settings demonstrate improved generative fidelity, strong cross-scale consistency, and substantial inference speedups over representative autoregressive and diffusion-based baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/kkking-kk/UniFlow

papers.title: Leakage-aware acoustic drone detection: fusing hand-crafted and pretrained audio features in a stacking ensemble
papers.abstract: Small multirotor drones produce a characteristic acoustic signature, and microphones offer a low-cost way to detect them. High accuracies have been reported on public drone audio benchmarks, often with random clip-level splits of datasets built from a few long recordings and pieces of existing sound collections, so pieces of one source can appear in both training and test data. We study the binary task of the public DroneAudioDataset (11,704 one-second clips). Its 1,332 drone clips come from 257 five-second chunks of 7 recordings, and 96.4% of its non-drone clips are pieces of the 2,000 clips of the ESC-50 sound dataset. A grouped, source-disjoint protocol (five folds, three repeats) is compared with a random split. Each clip is described by 57 hand-crafted acoustic descriptors, reduced by a hybrid minimum-redundancy maximum-relevance and ReliefF selection or by NSGA-II multi-objective search, and by a 1024-dimensional embedding from the pretrained YAMNet network. Random Forest and XGBoost learners on both views form a stacking ensemble. Under the grouped protocol, the two-view stack reached a mean accuracy of 95.29% (SD 1.62 points over 15 test folds), a specificity of 98.29% and an area under the ROC curve of 0.990, and it correctly classified 98.78% of unseen ESC-50 source clips as non-drone. The random split overstated accuracy by 1.89 to 3.22 points for the four models. Adding YAMNet embeddings to the hand-crafted view raised accuracy by 1.11 points (higher in 12 of 15 folds). Hybrid selection matched the accuracy of all 44 baseline descriptors with 16 to 18 features, and NSGA-II retained 4 to 6 features at lower accuracy. The stack took 51.0 ms per clip on one CPU thread. Source-disjoint evaluation exposes the optimism of random splits and gives a reliable benchmark, and fusing hand-crafted with YAMNet features consistently improves detection in real time on one CPU thread.

papers.title: Policy Network Diffusion
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have shown remarkable progress in AI-generated content, including images and videos. In this paper, we explore whether diffusion models can generate the parameters of policy networks in reinforcement learning (RL), and whether the generated policies exhibit generalization capabilities. To achieve this, we propose Diffusion-based Conditional Policy Network Parameter Generation (DPPG), which consists of a Transformer-based autoencoder and a task-conditioned diffusion model. The autoencoder achieves a high compression rate by patchifying network parameters, while the task-conditioned diffusion model generates corresponding parameters conditioned on different environments. Our experiments demonstrate that, with a single unified DPPG model, we can synthesize high-quality policies across a diverse set of tasks from different environment domains, including Classic Control, Atari games, and MuJoCo. Additionally, our method can generate networks with a larger number of parameters compared to previous approaches. Furthermore, we find that in previously unseen environments, DPPG can generate parameters that achieve faster convergence and reach competitive performance, showcasing the potential future applications of parameter generation via diffusion.

papers.title: CogniLife: Continuous Cognitive Distillation for Deployed Multi-Expert Agent Marketplaces
papers.abstract: Multi-expert agent marketplaces -- where creators publish domain-specific AI experts for end users to consult -- are an emerging deployment pattern for language technology. A published expert can receive many requests yet little evidence about its creator, who remains active elsewhere: the cold-expert problem. We frame continuous cognitive distillation as converting attributed creator observations into revisable decision rules, communication patterns, and domain procedures. CogniLife proposes a cross-expert attribution design for this problem, with Creator Profiles for transferable creator patterns and Expert Journals for listing-specific knowledge; this design is not yet implemented or evaluated. A deployed platform partially realizes the surrounding lifecycle through creator-authorized authoring, capability-owned proposal filtering, and reversible consolidation of eligible owner-scoped memory. On ProfyBench-v1, an 85-task offline benchmark built from replay seeds and controlled internal tests, the Profy Full configuration as a whole achieves a mean overall score of 4.65/5 from the primary LLM judge, compared with 4.01 for Raw LLM and 4.28 for Expert Prompt, with the largest gains in completeness, specificity, and missing-information tasks. These configuration-level scores do not test cold-expert mitigation, cross-expert transfer, or longitudinal distillation.

papers.title: Canonical Projectivization of Algebraic Varieties
papers.abstract: We construct canonical projective birational models of normal proper integral algebraic spaces over arbitrary fields. The construction preserves the intrinsic quasi-projective core and is natural under semilinear isomorphisms. For smooth proper integral input in characteristic zero, we combine an intrinsic choice of ideals with Włodarczyk's principalization to obtain a canonical tower of blowups in smooth centers ending in a smooth projective variety. Consequently, every compact connected Moishezon manifold admits a smooth projective bimeromorphic model to which all automorphisms lift compatibly. The main ingredient is a family-sum argument yielding an intrinsic finite selection of maximal tuples of boundary ideal germs; successive modifications strictly decrease the boundary-image dimension. We also construct canonical quasi-projective models for nonproper normal input and a greatest schematizing ideal for separated finite-type algebraic spaces over noetherian bases. Oda's threefold illustrates the construction.

papers.title: Quadratic Hubbard trees, automata, and ray connections
papers.abstract: We describe an algorithm that, given a postcritically finite quadratic polynomial, outputs a finite state machine whose regular language is the set of angles whose dynamical rays land on the Hubbard tree, generalizing an example of Milnor. We do this by extracting orbit portraits from angled internal addresses, and constructing a suitable Markov partition of angle intervals. A main application is computing direct ray connections between Hubbard trees in matings of quadratic polynomials, and understanding when ray connections between the trees first appear when moving along veins of the Mandelbrot set. If one of the mating parameters is fixed, we prove that first ray connections are picked up at parabolic parameters or tips of veins. We also prove that the locus of parameter pairs in two given veins for which there are no ray connections between the trees is open. Additionally, we show that there are no ray connections between small Julia sets in matings of locally connected rabbit tunings.

papers.title: Reconfigurable Antenna-Enhanced ISAC: A Unified Perspective on Electromagnetic Adaptation
papers.abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) enables sensing and communication (S&C) functions to share time, frequency, and hardware resources, offering an efficient paradigm for next-generation wireless systems. However, conventional fixed-configuration antenna (FCA) architectures provide limited flexibility in adapting the physical electromagnetic (EM) response of the end-to-end wireless link. This article develops a unified EM-adaptation perspective on reconfigurable antenna (RA)-enhanced ISAC systems. We distinguish transceiver-side (TSc-side) and environment-side (Env-side) RA deployments and identify five fundamental EM reconfiguration dimensions: position, orientation, radiation pattern, polarization, and frequency response. Building on this framework, we examine how these dimensions customize communication channels, actively control target information mapping for sensing, and reshape the interplay between S&C, particularly by improving compatibility between S&C requirements under shared resources. Two case studies illustrate how TSc-side and Env-side EM reconfiguration can improve spatial selectivity and the achievable S&C performance tradeoff. Finally, we discuss several promising directions for advancing RA-enhanced ISAC systems, including fundamental performance limits, low-overhead black-box optimization, and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled semantic ISAC.

papers.title: Finite-Sample Convergence in Networked Average Reward MARL: Decentralization Pitfalls and Entropy Remedies
papers.abstract: We study the problem of average reward Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) where agents interact within a network. Each agent in the network conducts local updates with information within its $k$-hop neighborhood and collaboratively maximizes the overall reward of the entire network. We first provide impossibility results in achieving convergence to the global optimal joint policies in our setting. These impossibility results highlight the challenges of decentralized learning with local information in multi-agent systems, namely the issues of multiagency, where each agent independently optimizes its policy, and partial observability, where agents have limited visibility into the global state. Given these challenges which indicate that decentralized policy optimization can generally be certified only up to stationarity, we provide finite-sample convergence guarantees for a decentralized actor-critic algorithm with linear function approximation that converges to an approximate stationary point with small gradient norm. To overcome such impossibility results, we further show that adding fixed-state entropy regularization reshapes the objective landscape which leads to even stronger global convergence guarantees for our proposed actor-critic algorithm.

papers.title: Counterexample-driven autonomous research with application to excess radiated energy in a Z-pinch
papers.abstract: Recent breakthroughs in artificial-intelligence-assisted mathematics show that open-ended machine search can outperform human mathematicians, yet transferring this paradigm to physics requires refactoring the research workflow. We introduce Simjecture, an open-source framework in which language-model agents pursue human-defined physical conjectures. The framework tackles two central challenges in this transfer: first, because physics is empirical and no model is final, it structures inquiry around counterexample-driven falsification and prospective hypothesis repair; second, because physical theories must interact with the real world, it uses computational physics as an executable testbed while separating the qualification of numerical instruments from scientific claim review so solvers and diagnostics can be adapted within a recorded investigation. We apply the framework in a 136.3 h investigation to tackle the long-standing problem of radiated energy exceeding the imploding-shell kinetic energy in a Z-pinch. The investigation reveals competing effects of energy conversion, retention, and release timing. Stronger coherent helical deformation increases resistive conversion while reducing radiation and increasing retained energy. In a matched fine-grid test, broadening the trailing-plasma profile delays the later radiation maximum by 1.80 ns and recovers an early 153 J bolometric deficit to within 0.08% by 44 ns, with a spectral response that shifts during the pulse. These results provide new insight into energy conversion in high-energy-density plasma physics and demonstrate a new paradigm for physics research.

papers.title: DiabAgent: Toward Agentic Physiological Control
papers.abstract: As pretraining scales, medical language models have advanced rapidly in clinical question answering. Their ability to achieve effective physiological control through sustained intervention still lacks systematic quantitative evaluation. Type 1 diabetes provides a concrete setting: impaired insulin secretion creates dependence on exogenous insulin, with dosing continually adjusted using information about meals, exercise, illness, and glucose measurements. We introduce DiabAgent, a research suite for agentic physiological control comprising the Agentic Physiological Control (APC) framework, the DiabetSim simulator, and the SweetBench benchmark. APC controls glucose through medical-device tools, using ongoing observations to infer individual states, accumulate personal experience, and choose treatment actions. We build DiabetSim to simulate different patients, events, and device conditions for scalable virtual testing and training. Using DiabetSim, we construct SweetBench by instantiating 32 scenario designs as 212 glucose-control tasks. With Claude Opus 5.5 and a fixed decision interval of one hour, APC achieves a COGI of 73.5, compared with 71.2 for the open-source closed-loop baseline OpenAPS. Ablations further show that individual adaptation and contextual information improve glucose control. Combining high-frequency rule-based control with lower-frequency agent decisions shows potential for balancing control performance and computational cost. Our work provides a framework, simulator, and evaluation foundation for agents to participate in human physiological control.

papers.title: DistDebug-Bench: Can LLM Agents Diagnose Bugs in Distributed Systems?
papers.abstract: LLM agents show strong potential in software engineering tasks such as competitive programming and code synthesis. Existing benchmarks, however, largely focus on small-scale settings such as self-contained Python modules, leaving distributed systems, an essential class of production software, under-examined. We introduce DistDebug-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' ability to diagnose complex-system failures at the code level. It curates 120 high-quality real-world bugs from 11 widely used distributed systems, spanning 5 programming languages and 10 failure patterns. Through an extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs and agents, we identify substantial gaps between current agents and real-world debugging tasks. A recurring gap is tunnel vision due to a lack of explicit reasoning structure and nondeterminism from inconsistent tool-use scope. The benchmark and evaluator are available at https://github.com/OrderLab/distdebug-bench, with agent traces and a leaderboard at https://distdebug.com.

papers.title: A Note on the Finite-Exceedance Dependence Principle for Sum--Maximum Asymptotic Independence
papers.abstract: Asymptotic independence between sum-type and maximum-type statistics arises repeatedly across many areas of probability and statistics, particularly in high-dimensional testing and random matrix theory. Motivated by the shared structure underlying existing proofs, which is obscured by their model-specific formulations, this note isolates a common intermediate principle. We introduce a finite-exceedance dependence principle: if the finite-exceedance dependence error vanishes at every fixed order and high-order exceedances are mildly controlled, then a finite-order Bonferroni argument yields asymptotic independence between the sum and the maximum. We further give an independent-proxy criterion for verifying this: for each finite set of exceedances, it suffices to construct an exactly independent proxy for the sum-type statistic whose approximation error is negligible in aggregate. Local deletion under dependency graphs and Gaussian regression and residualization are two examples. The framework gives modular derivations of existing sum--max independence results.

papers.title: Transgression branes in seven dimensions
papers.abstract: A seven dimensional theory with branes, described by a Transgression Action is investigated. The theory has special properties owing to the factorization of the trace used to define the Transgression form. It is shown that in some cases the theory is similar to the models of branes proposed by Nepomechie, Wu and Zee as a higher dimensional generalization of models of particles with fractional statistics of Wilczek, Wu and Zee. Static Euclidean solutions are presented, and compared with similar solutions of Nepomechie,Wu and Zee. Then Lorentzian static solutions are considered, based in solutions of constant curvature black holes presented by Bañados and further studied by Guilleminot, Olea and Petrov. Topological phases and their implications for quantum statistics are discussed.

papers.title: Charge-Activated Birefringence and Shadow Mimicry around Reissner-Nordström Black Holes
papers.abstract: We discover that electric charge can activates birefringence for a neutral vector field coupled to the Einstein tensor around a Reissner-Nordström black hole. Changing the electric charge of an uncoupled black hole can mimic one parity's shadow radius of a coupled black hole. The coupling makes the two parity looks differently. It separates their shadow edges of two parities and produces a backward-scattered signal with reversed helicity. However changing the charge alone cannot reproduce both effects. They require both nonzero charge and coupling. At weak coupling, the leading correction is the same for both potential. Positive coupling raises the potential, reduces low-frequency absorption and decrease the average shadow radius. Negative coupling reverses these trends. The backward signal is nonzero, this is due to the difference between the complex scattering amplitudes of the two parities. It is entirely helicity reversed. For the uncoupled field, the shadows is the same for both parities and the backward intensity vanishes exactly at every charge. We can use the split edge and backward signal to distinguish the coupling from a change of charge alone. A comparison with observations still requires a mechanism that produces and detects this field.

papers.title: Mechanical modulation of the Gutenberg-Richter b-value in hierarchical fault networks
papers.abstract: The Gutenberg-Richter (G-R) law is seismology's most robust empirical regularity, yet a unified mechanical explanation for its slope-the b-value-remains a subject of ongoing debate. Here, we propose a framework suggesting that the b-value is mechanically modulated by the hierarchical architecture of fault networks. By coupling fracture mechanics with hierarchical network topology, we derive a generalized closed-form expression: b=\frac{3}{3+2γ}\frac{\log_{10}k}{\log_{10}q}. We further link these topological parameters to rate-and-state friction theory, illustrating that k and q can be mechanistically constrained by the competition between elastic stiffness, frictional healing, and energy dissipation. The empirical universality of b=1 may arise as the system balances these competing mechanisms, tending to reside near a mechanically balanced state (k=q). Furthermore, the dynamic decoupling of k and q under tectonic loading drives the system away from this critical state, providing a mechanical explanation for observed b-value anomalies. The stress-drop scaling exponent γ enters as a modulated perturbation about the constant-stress (γ=0) zeroth-order baseline: it shifts b only where source-scaling data independently constrain γ away from zero. By establishing a mechanistic connection between macroscopic statistical variations and microscopic mechanical processes, this framework may provide a new perspective for interpreting fault dynamics.

papers.title: Toward an Evidence-Based Template for Agent Instruction Files: An Empirical Study of Adoption, Consistency, and Maintenance
papers.abstract: AI coding agents rely on repository-level instruction files to understand project conventions, development workflows, and constraints. However, different agents support different instruction formats, and limited empirical evidence exists about how these files are adopted, what information they contain, whether coexisting formats provide consistent guidance, and how they are maintained. We conduct an empirical study of 3,387 instruction files from 1,000 GitHub repositories across four formats: AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, GitHub Copilot instructions, and Cursor rules. We find that 42.2% of instruction-bearing repositories in the higher-popularity cohort maintain multiple formats. Among 386 manually examined pairs of corresponding sections, 16.1% provide divergent guidance. Our maintenance analysis further shows that 40.4% of the analyzed files have only one recorded modification event and that maintenance patterns differ across formats. Based on category prevalence and category addition ratios (CAR), we derive an evidence-based template containing ten Required, four Gap, and two Recommended categories. In an exploratory generation experiment, explicit template guidance increases structural category coverage from 18.7% to 82.8%. We further introduce AGIT-Instruct, a benchmark for evaluating instruction-file generation through structural coverage and content alignment. Across four generation configurations, retrieval-augmented generation achieves the highest full-file ROUGE-1 F1 of 0.459. A manual assessment of 278 generated category instances finds that 19.4% fully preserve and 61.2% partially preserve developer-written intent. Our findings provide empirical guidance for organizing and maintaining agent instruction

papers.title: The DynaCell Evaluation Suite for Dynamic 3D Virtual Staining of Live Cells
papers.abstract: Understanding how cells respond to perturbations over time is central to cell biology and drug discovery. Live-cell imaging captures the dynamics of perturbation-induced phenotypes in individual cells. While fluorescence imaging can visualize specific molecular phenotypes, labeling and repeated illumination often affect cell health. Virtual staining offers an alternative by predicting these fluorescence images from images acquired without fluorescent labels. Although many virtual staining models have been developed, their performance on volumetric time-lapse data remains poorly characterized. We address this gap with an evaluation suite for 3D time-lapse virtual staining of live cells. The suite combines paired 3D time-lapse images acquired with and without fluorescent labels, a set of baseline models, and three metric tiers measuring pixel-level fidelity, organelle segmentation performance, and single-cell phenotype similarity. Using this evaluation suite, we study metric and model behavior across 3 cell types, 2 microscopes, 4 organelles, and 3 perturbation states. We find that regression baselines better predict the spatial localization of target organelles, whereas the generative baseline better captures the distribution of phenotypes across cells. These differences expose trade-offs between structural and phenotypic fidelity that are obscured by single-metric evaluation and suggest how virtual staining models can be developed for diverse downstream tasks such as localization, segmentation, tracking, and phenotypic profiling. We release the curated datasets, baseline checkpoints, and evaluation code as part of DynaCell, a broader framework for image-based profiling of cell-state dynamics.

papers.title: A proof of the sharpness conjectures for all saturated fusion systems
papers.abstract: We prove the Díaz$\unicode[Arial]{x2013}$Park conjecture for sharpness of saturated fusion systems. More generally, for every saturated fusion system $\mathcal F$ over a finite $p$-group and every Mackey functor for $\mathcal F$ over the localisation $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ of the integers at $p$, the higher limits of its contravariant part over the centric orbit category vanish in all positive degrees. In particular, the subgroup and normaliser decompositions of every $p$-local finite group $(S,\mathcal F,\mathcal L)$ over the $\mathcal F$-centric subgroups are sharp. This answers in the affirmative a question in the list of important open problems in [M. Aschbacher, R. Kessar and B. Oliver, Fusion Systems in Algebra and Topology, Cambridge Univ. Press (2011)], and proves the sharpness conjecture stated in [M. Aschbacher and B. Oliver, Fusion systems, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (2016)] and Conjecture 1.2 of [E. Yalç$\unicode[Arial]{x131}$n, Higher limits over the fusion orbit category, Adv. Math. (2022)]. The proof is algebraic and does not rely on the classification of finite simple groups.

papers.title: On cylindrical directions of regular surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^4$ derived from contact with spherical cylinders
papers.abstract: We investigate the contact of regular surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^4$ with spherical cylinders $S^2(r) \times \mathbb{R}$. We introduce cylindrical directions of these surfaces, defined by the axes of spherical cylinders having degenerate contact with the surfaces, and show that these directions capture the ridge condition of projected regular surfaces under orthogonal projection along these directions.

papers.title: MAC-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Collaboration via Interconnected Tasks
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) tackle challenging tasks by dividing work among agents and coordinating their contributions toward shared objectives. Evaluating these systems therefore requires benchmarks that assess not only task-solving performance but also the ability to handle interdependent work. However, existing benchmarks often emphasize task difficulty without substantial collaboration requirements or evaluate only a limited range of predefined collaboration patterns. In this paper, we introduce MAC-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaboration through interconnected tasks. Rather than imposing predefined agent roles or communication protocols, MAC-Bench embeds collaboration requirements directly into task dependencies and shared-resource constraints. Specifically, we mine reusable collaboration structures from selected benchmark tasks at two levels. Local collaboration patterns capture recurring interactions among subtasks, while global task structures characterize how these interactions contribute to complete workflows. Through coarse-to-fine composition, these structures are recombined into task graphs combining different collaboration requirements. Tasks are instantiated in executable environments with automated verification of partial progress and complete task resolution.

papers.title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Lessons from Biological World Models for Testing Action Effects
papers.abstract: Whether an action-conditioned world model uses actions is usually checked by replacing or removing them and measuring lost accuracy. With biological experiments as the guiding case, we show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect. A second failure is specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence (cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame), the pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from $-17.3$ to $-6832$ as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Our preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field ($E\approx1.1\times10^{10}$). Tempering factors estimated from residuals can err by an order of magnitude, whereas a mixture over a fixed grid of factors needs no estimate and loses at most the logarithm of the grid size in log e-value relative to its best member. In a registered test on a diffusion world model for three Atari games released by others, the pooled test rejected in 0 of 96 units in which actions mattered and Kish and contrast tempering in 0 and 1, while the mixture rejected in 96; under an exact null, eight statistics made 0 rejections in 1,536 tests. Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol, or labelled exploratory.

papers.title: A secondary term in the first moment of primitive cubic Dirichlet L-functions
papers.abstract: P. Gao and L. Zhao obtained an asymptotic formula for the smoothed first moment of primitive cubic Dirichlet \(L\)-functions over \(\Q\) with conductors coprime to \(3\), with a main term of order \(Q\) and error \(O\left(Q^{\frac{7}{8}+\eps}\right)\) under the generalized Lindelöf hypothesis. Building on their double Dirichlet series, we assume the generalized Riemann hypothesis and separate an explicit secondary term of order \(Q^{\frac{5}{6}}\) in the same family, with error \(O\left(Q^{\frac{23}{28}+\eps}\right)\). We explicitly evaluate the secondary coefficient and prove that it is strictly negative. We also prove unconditionally that the secondary polynomial in the squarefree second moment of the natural cubic Hecke \(L\)-functions over \(\Q(\sqrt{-3})\) has degree one and strictly positive leading coefficient, which we evaluate explicitly.

papers.title: Floquet engineering of quantum relaxation
papers.abstract: Dynamical decoupling suppresses decoherence by averaging selected interactions between a quantum system and its environment. Here, we extend this notion through a general Floquet formalism that maps periodic control onto relaxation and dephasing channels. Environmental fluctuations are decomposed into Floquet components that sample the noise spectrum at distinct frequencies, with coupling strengths determined by control-induced Floquet coefficients. We experimentally investigate this approach using a single nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under multi-pulse control. By tuning the drive and detuning, we reshape the coupling to environmental fluctuations and create isolated operating points where the dominant decoherence channel vanishes, strongly suppressing Floquet dephasing. The resulting coherence enhancement follows the predicted Floquet coupling coefficients and can be shifted by modifying the control sequence. These results establish Floquet driving as a general framework for engineering transverse and longitudinal relaxation through the design of quantum control protocols.

papers.title: Dimensional dependence of critical phenomena in black hole interiors
papers.abstract: Black hole interiors exhibit a critical transition in which a perturbed inner horizon either survives or collapses into a spacelike singularity, but whether the exponent governing this transition depends on spacetime dimension has remained an open question. In this paper, we numerically investigate the interior dynamics of $D$ dimensional Reissner-Nordström (RN) black holes perturbed by a real scalar field. Strong perturbations destroy the null inner horizon and produce a spacelike singularity, whereas weaker perturbations preserve it with an areal radius that decreases as the perturbation amplitude increases. As the initial scalar field amplitude $p$ approaches its critical value $p^{*}$, the inner horizon radius decreases continuously to zero. Near criticality, this radius obeys the power law $r_{s}\propto|p-p^{*}|^γ$. In four dimensions, different initial scalar field profiles and initial RN black hole charges yield nearly identical critical exponents, $γ\simeq1/2$, supporting the universality of the scaling law. Within the investigated range $4\leq D\leq9$, the critical exponent decreases systematically with increasing spacetime dimension. The numerical results suggest the scaling relation $r_s\propto|p-p^{*}|^{1/(D-2)}$. This result establishes a new dimension-dependent universality class for interior black hole critical phenomena, distinct from the standard Choptuik collapse scaling.

papers.title: Dysfunctional Functionals and their Therapies in Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory
papers.abstract: The exchange-correlation functional in Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory (TDDFT) is known to have dependence on past densities and initial states, and yet this memory-dependence is ignored in practical calculations which almost always use an adiabatic approximation. We discuss the dysfunction that arises due to this deficiency and point to therapies that go beyond the adiabatic approximation. Still, adiabatic TDDFT has had success in a wide range of systems for response properties and for fully non-equilibrium dynamics, and why this is so is only partially understood. This, together with the rigorous foundation of the exact theory and its favorable system-size scaling, provides tremendous impetus for continuing to strive towards improved approximations to the exact functionals, and a deeper understanding of the impact of approximations in applications.

papers.title: Diagnosing Prototype Estimation in Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning: Training-Free Geometry Selection and Unlabeled-Query Prototype Rectification
papers.abstract: Frozen visual encoders make prototype heads competitive in few-shot class-incremental learning (FSCIL), but it remains unclear how much of the residual head gap is sensitive to noisy novel-class means rather than to the subsequent changes introduced by classifier refitting. On identical features, we construct a retrospective matched counterfactual: first replace each five-shot novel mean with its complete-data counterpart under fixed cosine scoring, then fit a linear probe. Across sixteen strong encoder dataset pairs, mean replacement accounts for the majority of this ordered gap. Shot and classwise diagnostics support a finite-sample mechanism, whereas a weaker base-only encoder does not satisfy the same criterion. This diagnosis motivates ShrinkSel, a support-only selector over prototype radius and covariance shrinkage whose family contains shared LDA as an exact fallback. Across sixteen evaluated pairs, it improves LDA on fifteen by 0.04-1.52 points and selects the exact LDA endpoint on Aircraft. We further introduce Query Prototype Rectification (QPR), a batch-transductive extension that uses gated unlabeled queries to update novel directions while preserving the selected geometry. On CLIP ViT-B/16, QPR adds 1.21-2.03 points; exact query-wise self-exclusion retains the benefit, showing that the gains do not require self-inclusion. The update repairs scarce novel prototypes at a measurable base-class cost and weakens with plentiful supports or very small cohorts. Thus, the evidence available for prototype estimation is a central constraint in frozen-feature FSCIL.

papers.title: Digital sovereignty in professional translation workflows: a case study of migrating from Windows to Linux
papers.abstract: This study examines digital sovereignty in professional translation through a screening of computer-assisted translation tools and translation management systems, and a case study of migrating a translator's workstation from Windows to Linux. The framework combines three principles - Control, Continuity and Exit - with three practical requirements: native Linux operation, independence from mandatory external services, and independent access to essential data and resources. Drawing on documentary evidence and the limited number of responses received from providers, the ecosystem screening distinguishes Linux accessibility from operational independence: browser-based platforms may remain dependent on provider-controlled infrastructure. The migration case demonstrates the feasibility of reconstructing one professional workflow around a locally operable Linux core, using LoopCAT, LibreOffice and locally run TranslateGemma, alongside tools for optical character recognition, communication, credential management and backup. Selected cloud services remained available where needed. The findings suggest that digital sovereignty depends on how workflow dependencies are organized, rather than on individual applications or operating systems. It does not require technological isolation, but meaningful control over essential components, continuity of work and practical exit options. The framework is tailored to the case examined here and may require adaptation to other professional workflows.

papers.title: DAPS: Dependency-Aware Premise Selection for LLM Theorem Proving
papers.abstract: LLM-based theorem proving in Lean 4 has advanced rapidly, but provers are difficult to leverage newly contributed lemmas, because retrieval skews toward popular foundational lemmas, leaving the right premises buried among hundreds of thousands of candidates. Existing neural selectors rank candidates by semantic similarity, with three intrinsic limitations: frequency-skewed retrieval, isolated pairwise ranking, and degradation on out-of-distribution queries such as competition problems and informal language. Given that mathematics is structured by dependencies rather than similarities, we restore this signal to both the training data and the model. We curate two underused dependency resources. We conduct the first systematic mining of 53 Lean Blueprint projects, a previously untapped corpus of 3,805 manually curated informal+formal nodes that capture rare, research-level premises absent from Mathlib4. We further pair it with the extraction of comprehensive, typed, multi-level Mathlib4 dependencies. We then introduce DAPS, a dependency-aware premise selector with a structural neighborhood encoder, a group-level contrastive objective, and a Mathlib-then-Blueprint adaptation procedure. DAPS reaches 78.74 Recall@16 on Mathlib4-Heldout (+11.41 over the strong selector LeanHammer) and widens the margin to 7xrecall on competition-style queries. Downstream, its selected premises raise Goedel-Prover-V2-8B Pass@4 on miniF2F-test from 49.90 to 54.03 and improve all four general-purpose LLMs on the informal IMO-ProofBench (up to +11.4% relative). Project page: https://daps-eth.github.io/.

papers.title: When AI Investigators Cannot Trust Their Tools: Conflict-Aware Evidence Verification for Cyber Threat Investigation
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly triage security alerts by combining the outputs of several detection tools, implicitly treating those tools as trustworthy. Unlike prior work on conflicts between a model's knowledge and its context, we study conflicts among the tools themselves: what happens when this machine-generated evidence is conflicting or wrong. On the corrected CIC-IDS2017 dataset, four heterogeneous detectors emit labels and confidences that we corrupt under a threat model varying the number of corrupted tools, the persistence of the corruption, and the confidence attached to wrong outputs. Across open-weight LLMs from 3B to 14B parameters, unverified investigators are fragile: one corrupted detector out of four lowers naive accuracy to .50-.72, three lower every unverified investigator to .13 or less, and honest disagreement alone makes them abstain on up to 63% of flows. We propose Conflict-Aware Evidence Verification (CAV), built from established components: an equal-weight vote that ignores reported confidences, an evidence-conflict gate, and an independent nearest-neighbour trust check that tests the leading candidates. With its prompt frozen before testing, CAV-LLM improves on the naive investigator in every corrupted condition ($p < 0.001$), reaching .84-.88 with three corrupted detectors against at most .08, while calling the LLM on 0.4% of clean traffic. A fixed verification rule is as accurate or better unless most tools are corrupted. When we make the independent channel itself noisy, CAV inherits its errors: it stays ahead when two or more tools are corrupted, but adding the channel as an extra voter is better when at most one is. Verification thus moves trust from the tools to the check, which must be measured and protected in turn.

papers.title: Two-peak gravitational wave spectra from supercooled two-field phase transitions
papers.abstract: We study the gravitational wave (GW) spectrum generated by supercooled first-order phase transitions in two-field conformal models. We construct three representative toy models that capture the essential features of these models, derive analytical criteria for the existence of two-step transitions, and show how the two-field dynamics generate a genuine two-peak GW spectrum. We identify regions of parameter space in which two-peak GW spectra are observable at LISA and the Einstein Telescope. By way of illustration, we apply our analysis to a realistic conformal dark SU(3) model.

papers.title: Higher-order derivatives and their applications to diffeomorphism groups
papers.abstract: In this paper, we apply higher-order tangent bundles and higher-order derivative maps to study countable subgroups of the diffeomorphism group ${\rm Diff}(M)$ of a closed smooth manifold $M$. Using this framework, we introduce the concept of higher-order $μ$-discreteness for subgroups $Γ< {\rm Diff}(M)$, and show that both the strong Novikov conjecture and the coarse Baum--Connes conjecture hold for countable groups with higher-order $μ$-discreteness. Finally, we give examples showing that higher-order $μ$-discreteness encompasses a strictly larger class of subgroups of $\operatorname{Diff}(M)$ than its lower-order counterpart.

papers.title: Incorporating Machine-Others: An Enactive Exploration of Human-LLM Interactions
papers.abstract: New concepts based in interactional thinking are required to understand how humans are changed by relating to LLMs. Standard theories of technological impact upon users' autonomy are inadequate here, because this technology is capable of inducing linguistic interactions with humans in an unprecedented manner. Traditional theories of social cognition also fall short, because LLMs have neither autonomy nor minds nor sociality as such. And yet, humans interact, talk, and create with them. We base ourselves on enactive theory, particularly on the theory of Linguistic Bodies and recent developments of enactive accounts of AI, to explore how we make sense with machines. We argue that we incorporate machine-others in two ways: in the tool-like sense of incorporation as enabling particular skills, but also in the more linguistic and identity-tied sense of incorporating (and incarnating) LLMs' ways of languaging. However, LLMs are themselves excorporated and excarnated phantoms of our own languaging; we give a (machinic) body to our language. As such, we are not just incorporating machinic others; we are incorporating excorporated others. These conceptual advances draw a new map of our linguistic relation to LLMs, putting them in continuation with other forms of languaging involving other linguistic artifacts (e.g., religious books). We attend to some particular forms that this relation takes today, and how they may be impacting the autonomy and becoming of LLM-engaged humans. We introduce the idea of "susceptive sense-making" to characterize increased semiotic labour that is carried by the lack of friction that we sometimes encounter within these services.

papers.title: Tight Asymptotic Bounds on the Size of Order Graphs
papers.abstract: Order graphs were introduced by Arroyuelo et al.\ (TODS 2024) as a generalization of the ring index, to support worst-case optimal joins on relations of arity $d$ while storing few columns: the index stores one column per edge, so its size is proportional to the number of edges of an order graph. It was known that the minimum number of edges lies between $Ω(2^d\sqrt d)$ and $O(2^d d)$, and the lower bound had been claimed to be $42$ for $d=6$. We first exhibit an optimal order graph with only $40$ edges for $d=6$, and show that the proof of that lower bound holds only for unions of cycles, whereas order graphs can be smaller than the smallest set of cycles. We give a corrected statement and proof that holds for every order graph: there must be at least $\max_m\binom dm\lceil m/2\rceil$ edges. This bound is $40$ (hence tight) for $d=6$. We then settle the asymptotic question: the minimum size is $Θ(2^d\sqrt d)$. This is obtained via an explicit construction, based on symmetric chain decompositions of the Boolean lattice, with at most $(d-1)\binom{d}{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}+2^d$ edges. The upper bound is within a factor $4+O(d^{-1/2})$ of the lower bound, and both numerically and asymptotically better than trie switching. Finally, we cast the problem as a set cover with connectivity constraints, which yields an exact ILP formulation and a greedy heuristic. With them we find optimal order graphs for $d\le 6$ in the bidirectional and for $d \le 7$ in the unidirectional model, showing that our lower bounds are tight there, and improve the best known order graphs for $d=7$ and $8$.

papers.title: Actuator-Aware Observer Inputs for Cascade ADRC of Quadrotors Under Rotor Lag, Measurement Delay and Sensor Noise
papers.abstract: In sampled cascade linear active disturbance rejection control (LADRC) of quadrotors, the extended-state observer receives the instantaneous command, although the delayed measurement reflects an earlier, rotor-filtered acceleration. This simulation and software-in-the-loop design study examines actuator-aware (AA) observer inputs: altitude and attitude observers use limited virtual inputs filtered by an assumed rotor model and aligned with the measurement delay, and horizontal observers use acceleration reconstructed from measured attitude. Fixed gains are selected on the discrete-time model under sensitivity and step-response requirements and stationary covariance ceilings on channel activity and on the noise-induced inner-loop increment of the full cascade. In paired set-point trials, PID-Budget, AA-Budget and AA-HalfGain reach mean RMSEs of 65.5, 19.2 and 16.9~mm; under a stricter common cascade ceiling, the AA designs reach 29.9 and 26.4~mm versus 72.3~mm for a PID with about twice their rotor-command increment. Ablations attribute the improvement to the rotor-lag model and the measured-attitude input; at the nominal 5-ms delay, delay alignment changes the RMSE by 0.013~mm. PX4 software-in-the-loop runs reproduce these results. Behind EKF2, a noise model fitted to the estimation errors predicts the roll/pitch and yaw increments within 5\%. After redesign for this stack, AA-Budget-E reduces the set-point RMSE from 59.1~mm (PID-E) to 44.0~mm with a lower rotor-command increment in every paired tracking run (S6: 45\% lower, 15\% after output quantization); AA-HalfGain-E beats PID-E only on the lemniscate. With fixed gains, the AA designs tolerate less unmodelled rotor lag and delay than PID in the linear sensitivity screen. The ceilings are nominal tuning constraints.

papers.title: Displacement Moments and Path-Terminal Separation in Brownian Interpolant Sampling
papers.abstract: We prove early-stopped, target-to-output KL guarantees for Brownian interpolant Euler sampling from the true source under arbitrary Borel couplings, even with nonintegrable endpoints. At fixed stopping time and noise level, a fourth displacement moment yields an $O(N^{-1})$ discretization term. A second moment suffices for fixed-law convergence with grid refinement and vanishing drift error. For one fixed coupling with no displacement moment above two, the original and comparison paths have KL of orders one and $1/\log N$ relative to the exact-drift Euler path. On the same geometric grid, terminal KL is at most $C/N^2$. The path decomposition identifies the information about the source discarded by Markov projection. When the original bridge is Markov, current-state Euler sampling has an $O((M_2+d)/N)$ discretization term. We prove expected stopped-output KL consistency for a learner trained on iid endpoint pairs with fresh true-source initialization. In a spatial image control, iterative sampling has worse fair energy scores than direct prediction with resampled residuals. Uniform terminal rates for general second-moment couplings remain open.

papers.title: Online Interval Selection with Binary Predictions: Optimal Consistency and a Continuous Robustness Tradeoff
papers.abstract: We study online interval selection with binary predictions of membership in a final optimal solution. Requests arrive in arbitrary order; accepted requests may be revoked, but rejected or revoked requests cannot be recovered. With rewards proportional to interval length, the best consistency under finite strict robustness is $d=(3+\sqrt5)/2$ when both guarantees hold almost surely on each fixed input, including for randomized algorithms. A continuous lower bound forces consistency strictly above $d$ at every robustness budget below $4φ+3\approx9.472$, whereas our deterministic algorithm attains $d$ with exact robustness $φ^5\approx11.090$, where $φ=(1+\sqrt5)/2$. Each held interval inherits a ledger recording positive prediction mass lost through irrevocable decisions. Tuning the replacement costs and both special thresholds gives a continuous family with exact consistency throughout and exact robustness on two parameter intervals, including $(C,R)=(25/9,10)$ and $(4,7)$. Randomization permits expected consistency approaching one with finite expected robustness, whereas almost-sure robustness forces expected consistency strictly above two at every finite budget.

papers.title: Climate change, sea level rise, and the agricultural revolution
papers.abstract: We test various hypotheses for the invention and spread of agriculture: higher temperatures, increased seasonality, sea level rise, and technological progress on the extensive margin. We successfully replicate Matranga (QJE 2024). His seasonality hypothesis survives alternative data, estimators, competing hypotheses, and, for adoption but not invention, bootstrap clustering. Population density played a role in the invention of agriculture, while spatial diffusion was important for its spread. Sea level rise and climate change had a minor effect on the population density of the areas that first adopted agriculture. Extrapolating a logit model for the invention of agriculture, some now-submerged areas in the Persian Gulf, Mediterranean, and Yellow Sea were suitable for early agriculture. Over time, technological progress was the main factor in extending agriculture's extensive margin.

papers.title: Explicit Serre weights for modular Galois representations of $U(2)$
papers.abstract: Let $p$ be an odd prime. Let $G$ be a rank two definite unitary group as defined by Barnet-Lamb et al. in [2]. In this article, we determine explicit modular local Serre weights for mod $p$ Galois representations $\barρ_h$ associated to eigenforms $h$ of $G$, with arbitrary weights and small slopes. As a consequence, we also determine modular global Serre weights in certain cases. We show analogous results for certain Hilbert modular eigenforms corresponding to totally definite and indefinite quaternion algebras. In proving our results, we identify the non-singular submodules in quotients of certain symmetric power $\mathbb{F}_q[\text{M}_2(\mathbb{F}_q)]$--modules by Dickson polynomials and their twisted versions.

papers.title: MVRCap: Towards Comprehensive Video Captioning via Hierarchical Multi-Dimensional Verifiable Rewards
papers.abstract: Despite significant progress, current models struggle to generate comprehensive video captions, constrained primarily by coarse-grained supervision, which often fails to capture spatial-temporal dynamics and the underlying logical intent. To address this issue, we introduce MVRCap, a novel framework that reformulates video captioning as a reinforcement learning task steered by structured verification. Central to our approach is a Fine-Grained Verifiable Reward mechanism, serving as dense supervision to enforce rigorous visual-semantic alignment. Specifically, we construct this reward system anchored by three complementary pillars: a Hierarchical Concept Coverage Reward utilizing our newly constructed MVRCap-QA dataset to ensure multi-dimensional completeness and semantic depth, a Factuality Verification Reward to enhance factual consistency, and a Conciseness Constraint to maximize semantic density. Furthermore, we curate the high-quality MVRCap-SFT dataset, providing structured annotations across six key dimensions, to serve as a robust foundational initialization for the RL policy in this training pipeline. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MVRCap achieves state-of-the-art performance on authoritative benchmarks including VDC, CAPability, and VC4VG.

papers.title: Diameter Bounds and Finiteness of Graphs from Local Intersection Data
papers.abstract: We extend the Bakry--Émery curvature framework on graphs, broadening its applications and strengthening the resulting diameter bounds. We study diameter bounds and finiteness for amply regular graphs, distance-regular graphs, $(s,c,a,k)$-graphs, and locally strongly regular graphs. In particular, for an amply regular graph with parameters $(v,k,λ,μ)$, we prove that \[{\rm{diam}}(G)\le4+8\log\frac{k}{\max\{λ,μ\}}\] when $μ>2$ and $k\ge3λ^2/μ$, improving the previous linear bound $4k/(λ+4)$ to a logarithmic bound. We also address several related conjectures. In their monograph \emph{Distance-Regular Graphs}, Brouwer, Cohen, and Neumaier conjectured that every amply regular graph with $μ>1$, except the icosahedron, satisfies ${\rm{diam}}(G)\le2k/(λ+2)$. We confirm this bound when $μ>λ+1$ and give counterexamples to the conjecture with $μ=λ$. For amply regular graphs with $μ\geλ$ and $μ>1$, we obtain ${\rm{diam}}(G)\le 2k/μ+1$. This proves the Qiao--Park--Koolen conjecture. In 1983, Terwilliger conjectured that every $(s,c,a,k)$-graph with $c>1$ is finite. We prove this conjecture when ``$s>2$, $c>2$, $(s,c)\ne(4,3)$'' and when ``$s=2$, $c>7$''. Moreover, we prove Weetman's finiteness conjecture for locally strongly regular graphs when the local parameter $μ>1$, and disprove his stronger conjecture that every strongly regular graph is an $\mathscr{S}$-graph. We also prove that every graph whose local graphs all have rank 3 is finite, which in particular proves a conjecture of Soicher in 1992.

papers.title: How Tuning, Reference Preview, Actuator Modeling, and Fallback Policies Change Quadrotor Controller Comparisons: A Reproducible Simulation Study
papers.abstract: Quadrotor controller comparisons commonly report a single tracking error, although the ranking also depends on tuning effort, reference information, actuator prediction, optimizer fallback, and command timing. We quantify these effects for cascade PID, hover LQR, boundary-layer sliding-mode control (BL-SMC), linear MPC with LQR fallback (LMPC-F), a preview-enabled LMPC-F, and a geometric $SO(3)$ controller on a common nonlinear plant with rotor gyroscopic coupling, motor lag, and saturation. A primary study (556 episodes at 50~Hz) combines matched twelve-candidate tuning, 400 paired evaluation episodes, and a 48-cell MPC factorial; a confirmation study (1462 episodes) repeats the evaluation on 50 fresh realizations with tuning budgets of 12, 24, and 48 candidates. A matched twelve-candidate tuning protocol changed the mean-RMSE ordering of the fixed baseline settings, mainly by moving BL-SMC from last to first. The ordering recurred on fresh realizations and did not change with 48 candidates, although BL-SMC's lead on the fresh set depends on a wider search range for its vertical switching gain. Reference preview reduced MPC tracking error and removed fallback activity on the figure-eight task. In single abrupt-step runs, completion depended jointly on fallback policy, predictor, and actuator authority. Command timing also changed the outcome: replaying measured command-call delays terminated three of four nominal MPC configurations on a desktop and all four on a Raspberry Pi~5, whereas capping the solver at 100 iterations removed every deadline miss in these profiles. We propose a reporting checklist that adds tuning effort, failure rates, fallback activity, applied-input variation, and command timing to tracking accuracy.

papers.title: A nonstandard selfinjective algebra of Euclidean type
papers.abstract: Let $\Bbbk$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic different from $2$. We realize the four-dimensional selfinjective algebra $Ω(1)$ as an admissible infinite cyclic orbit algebra of the repetitive Kronecker category. Thus an algebra long stated to be nonstandard is of Euclidean type in the orbit-algebra sense. We also identify a gap in an earlier proof of its nonstandardness and give an independent proof by determining all connected Galois covering sources of $Ω(1)$. Together, these results disprove the implication from Euclidean type to standardness in the equivalence explicitly stated by Bocian--Holm--Skowroński (2004) and Bocian--Skowroński (2005). They also contradict the standardness conclusion of the Proposition in \S2.1 of Skowroński (1989); its main theorem in \S1.5 assumes standardness and is not contradicted by this example.

papers.title: Minimax Regret for Sobolev Kernel-Based Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: We study the minimax regret rate for episodic kernel-based reinforcement learning, where the expected reward and transition density belong to a Sobolev reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), with continuous state and action spaces, and adversarial initial states. For Sobolev smoothness parameter $ν>0$, state dimension $d_S$, and action dimension $d_A$, we prove that the minimax expected regret over $T$ episodes is $\widetildeΘ(T^{\max\{e_A,e_B\}})$, where $e_A=\frac{ν+d_A}{2ν+d_A}$, $e_B=\frac{ν+d_A+3d_S/2}{2ν+d_A+2d_S}$ with the other model parameters fixed. The two exponents reflect the distinct difficulties of action selection and learning across states. We introduce Sobolev Optimal Value Iteration (\texttt{SOVI}), which attains this rate from observed rewards and transitions. For fixed smoothness and reference-kernel lengthscale, its regret bound has a prefactor polynomial in the state-action dimension $d=d_S+d_A$, horizon $H$, reward and transition RKHS norm bounds $B_r,B_p$, and the norm-comparison factor $Λ$, up to logarithmic factors; $Λ=1$ for normalized Matérn kernels. The algorithm separates initial action selection from continuation-value estimation and combines local polynomial approximation with the shared RKHS structure of the approximation errors. Our matching upper and lower bounds determine the optimal dependence on the number of episodes for Sobolev kernel-based reinforcement learning regret minimization. Thus, we partially address the open problem in Vakili(2024) under Sobolev kernel RL.

papers.title: Massive Scalar Quasinormal Modes and Quasibound States of Charged Black Holes with Logarithmic corrections
papers.abstract: We study how long-range deformations in a black-hole metric affect the oscillation, trapping, and decay of a neutral, minimally coupled massive scalar field. We choose a logarithmic deformation of Reissner-Nordström (RN) sourced by nonlinear electrodynamics, arising as an exact solution of Einstein gravity. The same geometry also arises in a phenomenological perfect-fluid dark-matter model. We provide several exact completions of this geometry with finite Arnowitt-Deser-Misner (ADM) mass. Focusing on the original logarithmic geometry, we analyze both quasinormal modes (QNMs), which describe relaxation, and quasibound states (QBSs), which describe trapped modes with small horizon absorption. We first show that a small scalar mass moves the potential barrier outward, raises it, and reduces its curvature. First-order WKB then predicts weaker damping at every fixed finite multipole and overtone. We then compare several approaches, namely sixth-order WKB, global matching, a generalized Leaver method (adapted to the logarithmic geometry) and time-domain evolution. All methods yield consistent QNM estimates within their ranges of validity. Global matching and Leaver also agree closely for QBSs. Further analytic estimates with a reference trapped state show that a local Padé approximation gives a binding-energy error of about $0.04\%$, while leading Gamow tunnelling underestimates damping by about $25\%$. Across the sampled QBSs, increasing the scalar mass or nonlinear coupling strengthens binding but shortens the lifetime through greater horizon absorption. Finally, using an appropriate horizon regularization and a common complex radial contour, we demonstrate orthogonality of an independently computed QNM-QBS pair using a suitable relativistic bilinear framework.

papers.title: TrackTok: Object-Centric Video Tokenization with Semantically Persistent Tokens
